lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: Which of the following scenarios would be a contraindication to endoscopy?

options.html: Patient had a history of myocardial infarction 5 months ago
Patient had abdominal surgery 8 months ago
Patient’s abdominal x-ray shows free air
Patient is unable to consent to procedure, so consent is obtained from their substitute decision maker

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Free air on an abdominal x-ray is indicative of a hollow viscous perforation and necessitates an urgent surgical consultation and is an absolute contraindication to endoscopy which could make the problem worse. One needs to exercise caution in patients with recent surgery or MI but in this instance they happened remotely enough that they should not be an issue and consent from a substitute decision maker is valid when patient isn’t able to consent themselves.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: You are seeing a young male patient with refractory nausea and vomiting. He is a chronic marijuana user. What symptom would make you most suspect the patient has Cannabis Hyperemesis Syndrome?

options.html: His symptoms are worsening despite decreasing marijuana use
His symptoms are cyclical in nature with periods of good days and bad days
His marijuana stimulates his appetite and then he gets post prandial vomiting
He gets symptomatic relief from a hot bath or shower

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Relief from a hot bath or shower is highly suggestive of cannabis hyperemesis syndrome. Decreasing marijuana use should result in an improvement of symptoms in CHS, CHS may result in cyclic vomiting but is often continuous, and post prandial vomiting is not specific to any particular diagnosis of vomiting.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: When is the best time to take a proton pump inhibitor?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Acid secretion occurs via insertion of proton pumps in the gastric mucosa, which is triggered by ingestion of food. Thus, for a proton pump inhibitor to work most effectively, one needs to take it before a meal so that it is in the bloodstream at the time of food ingestion to block the insertion of proton pumps. If taken during a period of fasting, there is minimal proton pump activity and thus minimal inhibition will occur.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: A 70 year old male patient develops a peptic ulcer. Which of the following scenarios may complicate his presentation

options.html: He presents to the Emergency department with melena stool
He develops worsening abdominal pain and is diagnosed with pancreatitis
He present to the Emergency department with sepsis and is found to have a hollow viscous perforation in his abdomen.

answer:
The correct answer is E.

Remember complications of peptic ulcer disease include the acronym HOPP (hemorrhage, obstruction, perforation or penetration (ie. Pancreatitis, etc). Thus all of the above may occur.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: All of the following are mechanisms that may contribute to gastroesophageal reflux disease except…?

options.html: Patient is on a Beta Blocker medication

answer:
The correct answer is B.

A hypotensive LES & Hiatus hernia are both anatomic factors that may increase the risk of regurgitation of stomach contents. Pregnancy increases intraabdominal pressure which can also increase regurgitation. Weak peristalsis leads to poor clearance of acid reflux from the esophagus which may also increase symptoms. B-blockers really don’t have a significant impact on GERD symptoms (unlike Ca Channel blockers, which may decrease LES pressure!).

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: From the list below select which molecules or hormones are stimuli for gastric acid secretion (you may select more than one)?
answer:
The correct answer is B, D, G.

Parietal cells are the major source of acid secretion and they have 3 major receptors that triggers acid secretion: gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine. PPIs are highly efficacious because they are downstream of these receptors and thus block all 3 mechanisms of acid secretion. H2 receptor antagonists on the other hand, block only 1 of the 3 mechanisms of acid secretion and thus there is a higher risk of residual acidity with those agents.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Absorption, Diarrhea, IBD & Luminal Malignancy
lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: Which of these test results is most useful to rule out celiac disease?

options.html: Normal duodenal biopsy in a patient on a strict gluten-free diet
Absence of HLA DQ2 or HLA DQ8 in a patient on a strict gluten-free diet
Normal terminal ileal biopsy in a patient on a gluten-containing diet
Negative anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody in a patient with IgA deficiency

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Biopsies can be normal in a patient on a gluten free diet as can TTG antibodies if a person has an IgA deficiency so none of these would reliably exclude celiac. Celiac patients almost always have at least one of either DQ2 or DQ8 haplotypes, and thus their absence, is effective at ruling out celiac (NB: test also not altered by gluten free diet).

weekLabel: Week 11 - Absorption, Diarrhea, IBD & Luminal Malignancy
lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: A 40-year-old patient comes to your office with abdominal pain and chronic diarrhea. Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is at the top of your differential, until the patient presents with which of the following red flag sign or symptom?

options.html: Abdominal pain that improves with defecation

answer:
The correct answer is B.

The only red flag symptom/sign in the list is anemia. All the rest of the clues are very non specific symptoms. Other red flag symptoms include bright red blood per rectum, nocturnal stooling and weight loss.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Absorption, Diarrhea, IBD & Luminal Malignancy
lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: A patient presents to your clinic with abdominal pain and diarrhea for the last 6 months. The diarrhea is watery in nature and can occur day or night. They have lost about 15 pounds of weight over this time. Their vitals are stable and aside from some abdominal tenderness have a relatively normal physical exam. You order some laboratory tests which shows their Hemoglobin is 125 mg/l (N=125-145), WBC 12.4 mg/l (N=4-10), CRP 45 (N<5), Ferritin 5 (N=30 -300), B12 88 (N>200). The most likely diagnosis is:

options.html: Crohn’s Disease affecting the terminal ileum
Ulcerative colitis with left sided colitis

answer:
The correct answer is D.

This is not likely irritable bowel syndrome given the weight loss and abnormal lab tests. Not likely Ulcerative colitis given the lack of blood. Symptoms are most consistent with Crohn’s of the terminal ileum given lack of blood and low B12, since B12 absorbed in the terminal ileum.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Absorption, Diarrhea, IBD & Luminal Malignancy
lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: Causes of constipation include all of the following except:
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Common secondary causes of constipation include opioids, hypercalcemia & hypothyroidism (NOT hyperthyroidism). If no obvious secondary cause, then it may just be functional constipation (idiopathic).

weekLabel: Week 11 - Absorption, Diarrhea, IBD & Luminal Malignancy
lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: All of the following may be implicated as mechanisms of functional GI disorders except:

options.html: Increased lymphocytes in the intestinal mucosa

answer:
The correct answer is C.

In functional GI disorders, the intestinal mucosa should look normal under a microscope and there should be no increase in the intestinal lymphocytes. All the other mechanisms have been postulated to play a role in functional symptoms.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Absorption, Diarrhea, IBD & Luminal Malignancy
lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: What is the pathogenesis of diarrhea caused by Cholera?

options.html: cholera toxin activates CFTR receptor causing chloride secretion
cholera toxin invades distal small bowel enterocytes causing cell destruction
cholera toxin invades colonic cells causing dysentery
cholera toxin inactivates pancreatic lipase causing steatorrhea

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The cholera toxin acts in both the small and large bowel on CFTR receptors promoting chloride secretion and consequently Sodium secretion to maintain electric neutrality. This increases intraluminal osmolality, promoting fluid secretion into the lumen and impaired resorption of fluid, leading to profound watery diarrhea.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Absorption, Diarrhea, IBD & Luminal Malignancy
lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: Which of the following statements regarding cancers of the GI tract is false?

options.html: The vast majority of colon cancer is preventable
Patients with gastric cancer typically develop early symptoms
Almost all colon cancers arise from polyps
Squamous cell cancer is the most common type of esophageal cancer worldwide
Inflammatory bowel disease is a risk factor for colon cancer

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Unfortunately patients with gastric cancer don’t usually develop symptoms until the disease is quite advanced, so option B is the false statement. Through screening programs, colon cancer can largely be prevented, colon cancer usually goes through a polyp to cancer sequence, and inflammatory bowel disease with colonic involvement (classically UC) is a risk factor for colon cancer. Worldwide squamous cell cancer of the esophagus is the most common however adenocarcinoma is more common in the Western world.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Absorption, Diarrhea, IBD & Luminal Malignancy
lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: A 30 year old male with Crohn’s disease develops increasing abdominal pain and diarrhea for the last 10 days. The pain is in the right lower quadrant. On physical exam you note he has a fever at 38.5C, BP 115/74, HR 90, O2 Saturation 99%. As you palpate his abdomen you note significant tenderness and a fullness in the right lower quadrant. His bloodwork shows a white blood cell count of 21 (N=4-10) and CRP = 250 (N<5). The most likely complication of his Crohn’s that has developed is:
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The localized pain, fever, abdominal mass and elevated white blood cell count and significantly elevated CRP all point to an intra-abdominal abscess. Enterocolic fistula may present with worsening diarrhea but not necessarily the fever and such an elevated CRP. A stricture would present with more obstructive type symptoms and colon cancer is less likely in a 30 year old patient and there is no mention of weight loss which would be more typical of colon cancer.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Absorption, Diarrhea, IBD & Luminal Malignancy
lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: All of the following are indicated to treat Esophageal Variceal bleeding except:
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Medical treatments of variceal bleeding includes PPI therapy, octreotide & antiobiotics. Endoscopic treatments are variceal band ligation and possibly sclerotherapy. Radiologic treatments include TIPS. Thus by process of elimination, APC is not a typical treatment for variceal bleeding – this is typically used instead for angioectasia’s or GAVE.

weekLabel: Week 11 - Absorption, Diarrhea, IBD & Luminal Malignancy
lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: Which of the following colon cancer syndromes is usually associated with mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Hamartomatous & serrated polyposis syndromes may be caused by mutations in other genes.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: Which of the following are decompensating features of liver cirrhosis?

options.html: Ascites, jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, and variceal bleeding
Jaundice, ascites, malnutrition, and hepatic encephalopathy
Hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, hypoalbuminemia, and ascites
Malnutrition, ascites, variceal bleeding, and jaundice

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and hepatorenal syndrome are all decompensating features of cirrhosis. Decompensation is defined as an acute worsening of liver function. Malnutrition and hypoalbuminemia are frequently present in cirrhosis but are not specifically signs of decompensation

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: A 19-year-old female is referred to your office to further investigate an elevated TB of 55. She is otherwise healthy and is not currently taking any medications or herbal supplements. Physical exam is unremarkable. Repeat bloodwork shows Total Bilirubin 45, Direct Bilirubin 4.6. HB is 140, MCV 95, AST 20, ALT 30, ALP 65, ALB 40, LDH 200, and INR 1.0. Haptoglobin is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

This is predominantly an elevation in unconjugated bilirubin. The normal hemoglobin and LDH levels make hemolysis unlikely. B12 deficiency should not elevate bilirubin. The normal liver enzymes argue against hepatobiliary pathology. Crigler-Najjar usually presents with more severe elevations in bilirubin and would usually be discovered during infancy or early childhood as it can be fatal. Thus, that leaves Gilbert’s, which is typically a milder elevation in unconjugated bilirubin due to decreased levels of the enzyme which conjugates bilirubin (in Crigler-Najjar this enzyme is typically completely absent).

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: A 40-year-old female with a history of alcoholism presents to the hospital with acute onset of abdominal pain associated with nausea. She has an elevated lipase level and a CT of the abdomen showing edema of the pancreas and fat stranding and is diagnosed with acute pancreatitis. She is admitted for 4 days and then discharged home as she is improving clinically. Approximately 6 weeks later, she returns to the hospital with increasing abdominal pain. She is afebrile and hemodynamically stable. She has a normal lipase level. She undergoes a repeat CT of the abdomen which shows a large fluid collection adjacent to the pancreas. The most likely complication that has developed is:
answer:
The correct answer is E.

This is a very typical history for a pancreatic pseudocyst which often develops weeks after an episode of acute pancreatitis. It is not likely to be infected necrosis or abscess as she would likely be unwell & febrile with this. Pancreatic cancer is unlikely as she had no sign of this on CT scan 6 weeks prior. Chronic pancreatitis would not explain the fluid collection on CT.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: A 79-year-old female has a longstanding history of PBC cirrhosis. She has been stable for many years, but recently has developed ascites over the last 6 months. She started with restricting salt but continues to have ongoing fluid retention. She was started on furosemide and spironolactone with doses titrated up to 80 mg and 200 mg PO daily respectively. She cannot tolerate further dose escalation due to hypotension. She has no history of hepatic encephalopathy. Bloodwork shows an AST 40, ALT 50, ALP 400, Bilirubin 30, INR 1.1, ALB 34, HB 120, PLT 70, and CR 80. Which of the following options would be the next most appropriate management strategy for her?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

She has refractory ascites at this point given diuretics have been maxed out to the point of side effects. TIPS is indicated for treatment of refractory ascites as there are no contraindications such as hepatic encephalopathy. Her cirrhosis is otherwise well compensated, and she is 79 years old so would not be a transplant candidate. Serial paracentesis could be used as a bridging measure but is not definitive treatment.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: Which of the following is not part of the King’s College Criteria for liver transplantation for acetaminophen acute liver failure?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

King’s college criteria for liver transplantation for acetaminophen induced liver failure includes: an arterial pH < 7.3 OR all 3 of the following: INR>6.5, Creatinine > 300 and presence of Grade III or IV encephalopathy.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: A 25-year-old female is referred to your clinic with elevated transaminase liver enzymes. She has a history of intravenous drug use with last use 1 week ago. Prior liver enzymes from 3 months ago were normal. She has been feeling weak and fatigued for the last month. She denies any sick contacts or recent travel. Past medical history includes an abscess requiring debridement. She is not currently on any medications. Her vitals show T36.9*C, BP 134/82, HR 90, RR 16, 02 sat 99%. Bloodwork shows an ALT 300, AST 200, ALP 120, Total Bilirubin 44, INR 1.2, and ALB 41. Hepatitis A IgM is negative. Hepatitis B surface antigen is reactive and hepatitis B surface antibody is non-reactive. Hepatitis C antibody is nonreactive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

This appears to be an acute hepatitis given the clinical scenario and normal liver enzymes 3 months ago. With positive hepatitis B surface antigen, this is likely to be an acute hepatitis B. There is nothing in the history to suggest drug induced (she is not on any medications) or Ischemic hepatitis (there is no history of hypotension). Its not chronic hepatitis B as we already indicated this was likely an acute presentation. Gallstones, specifically choledocholithiasis, is a possibility but it is predominantly a hepatocellular picture and not cholestatic and we don’t have any imaging to support or refute this diagnosis.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: A 75-year-old male is seen in your clinic with painless jaundice which started 2 weeks ago. He has been complaining of a vague epigastric abdominal pain and early satiety for the last couple of months. He has lost 40 lbs. He has a history of osteoarthritis and acid reflux for which he takes naproxen and lansoprazole. On physical exam he is jaundice and cachectic. Abdominal exam was unremarkable. Bloodwork would show AST 100, ALT 133, ALP 800, GGT 400, Total Bilirubin 400, Direct Bili 300, INR 1.3, ALB 30, and CR 90. Which additional bloodwork will most likely confirm the diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

This scenario paints a picture concerning for malignancy with obstruction of the bile duct either cholangiocarcinoma or cancer at the head of the pancreas (painless jaundice with weight loss and elevated cholestatic enzymes). The tumor marker that may be elevated with pancreatic cancer or cholangiocarcinoma is CA 19-9.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: A 40-year-old female presents to your office with right upper quadrant pain for the last 2 weeks that waxes and wanes. It radiates to the back and is described as a sharp pain. It is worst after eating. She has had some episodes of nausea and vomiting. She has not had any fevers. Past medical history includes obesity and an appendectomy. She is not currently on any medications. Physical exam is unremarkable. AST is 39, ALT 42, ALP 120, Total Bilirubin 15, INR 1.1, ALB 45, Lipase 35. Ultrasound is pending. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

This is painting a picture typical of biliary colic (RUQ pain after eating, female, obese and has a mild elevation in ALP). Given she is afebrile it is unlikely to be ascending cholangitis or acute cholecystitis (although an ultrasound would be necessary to confirm). The normal bilirubin argues against choledocholithiasis. The normal lipase argues against pancreatitis.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: Elevated amylase levels are not specific to make a diagnosis of pancreatitis. All of the following can be associated with elevated amylase levels except:
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Elevated amylase can occur in the setting of pancreatic disease as well as salivary disease (ie. Parotitis), Gastrointestinal disease (ie. Bowel obstruction), Gynecologic disease (ie. Ovarian Cancer), or due to impaired clearance (ie. Renal failure). It is not however routinely associated with Portal Vein Thrombosis.

lectureMeta: The week's quiz, as it was sat.
stem: Total parenteral nutrition would be indicated in all of the following patients except:

options.html: Sustained an abdominal trauma requiring bowel resection leaving 70 centimeters of small bowel and a small part of the colon
Is malnourished, has a severe post-operative ileus of the bowel that has lasted 5 days
Is malnourished, had a stroke causing severe oropharyngeal dysphagia that requires them to be NPO
Is malnourished, has severe gut dysmotility and failed enteral tube feeding

answer:
The correct answer is C.

In the scenario of a stroke with oropharyngeal dysphagia, there is no reason why a feeding tube cannot be used to address the issue and thus is more appropriate than TPN. In all the other scenarios, there are structural issues with the GI tract that limit ability to absorb nutrition and thus require TPN.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding epithelial cells of the stomach lining
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Parietal cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factor. Mucus cells primarily secrete mucus and bicarbonate.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: You find yourself in a state of panic and your sympathetic nervous system is taking over. Which of the following actions describe the correct physiology in this state?

options.html: Your sympathetic nervous system releases norepinephrine which increases motility and secretion of the GI tract
Your sympathetic nervous system releases acetylcholine which increases motility and secretion of the GI tract
Your sympathetic nervous system releases acetylcholine which decreases motility and secretion of the GI tract
Your sympathetic nervous system releases substance P which decreases motility and secretion of the GI tract
Your sympathetic nervous system releases norepinephrine which decreases motility and secretion of the GI tract

answer:
The correct answer is E.

The sympathetic system releases norepinephrine which in turn decreases motility, secretions, blood flow, and delays gastric emptying. In a relaxed state the parasympathetic system relies on acetylcholine to increase motility and secretion to process food throughout the GI tract.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Several different hormones affect secretion and motility within the gastrointestinal tract. Which statement below is true?

options.html: Cholecystokinin reduces the rate of emptying of the stomach.
Motilin reduces motility within the digestive tract.
Gastrin reduces the secretion of gastric acid in the stomach.
Secretin reduces the secretion of bicarbonate from the pancreas.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Cholecystokinin is a hormone that induces the pancreas to secrete digestive enzymes, and the stomach to reduce the rate of emptying. Motilin increases gut motility; gastrin increases the secretion of gastric acid; and secretin increases the secretion of bicarbonate from the pancreas.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which statement below correctly identifies the substance that an epithelial cell secretes into the lumen of the GI tract?

options.html: Parietal cells secrete mucus into the stomach
Goblet cells secrete mucus into the small intestines
Paneth cells secrete serotonin into the small intestines
Chief cells secrete trypsinogen into the stomach

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Parietal cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factors. Goblet cells secrete mucus into the small intestine. Paneth cells secrete antibacterial factors into the small intestine (enteroendocrine cells secrete serotonin into the small intestines). Chief cells secrete pepsinogen into the stomach. Note that trypsinogen is secreted by the pancreas.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following hormones have a stimulatory effect on the intestinal motility but an inhibitory effect on stomach motility?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

CCK is a hormone which is secreted in the duodenum primarily to stimulate the digestion of fat and protein. It has a stimulatory effect on intestinal motility while having an inhibitory effect on stomach motility by delaying gastric emptying. Acetylcholine, gastrin and serotonin both have a stimulatory effect on intestinal and stomach motility. Norepinephrine is primarily a neurotransmitter of the sympathetic system and has an inhibitory effect on intestinal and stomach motility.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which neurotransmitter or hormone does NOT increase the rate that foodstuffs move through the small and large intestines?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Epinephrine reduces contraction in the small and large intestines. One helpful way to remember this is that epinephrine is a neurotransmitter associated with the sympathetic nervous system. When the sympathetic nervous system is activated, the body enters fight-orflight mode and digestion slows down.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Choose the correct sentence in relation to the anal sphincter

options.html: The internal anal sphincter is voluntary because it is under autonomous control.
The internal anal sphincter is voluntary because it is under somatic control.
The external anal sphincter is voluntary because it is under autonomous control.
The external anal sphincter is voluntary because it is under somatic control.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The internal anal sphincter is an involuntary muscle, under autonomous control. The external anal sphincter is under somatic control and is therefore voluntary.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: A patient with suspected oropharyngeal dysphagia is referred by their family physician to an otolaryngologist for further assessment. Which of the following concerns is the most concerning/necessary to workup during an assessment?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The primary reason for a workup is to assess the risk of Aspiration, as aspirated food items can be immediately life threatening.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which symptom is associated with functional oropharyngeal dysphagia?

options.html: Feeling of food stuck in the chest

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Oropharyngeal dysphagia is associated with drooling, food sticking in throat, weight loss, and increased meal duration. Food lodged in the throat presents an aspiration risk, which can lead to pneumonia.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following questions would you ask a patient with dysphagia to best distinguish oropharyngeal dysphagia from esophageal dysphagia?

options.html: Do you have difficulty initiating swallowing or after the action of swallowing?
Do you have difficulty swallowing solid and liquid foods or just solid foods?
Have you encountered any new lumps or bumps in your oral or neck region?
Is the difficulty swallowing progressive or intermittent?

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Esophageal dysphagia is primarily characterized by difficulty swallowing after the initiation of swallowing initiated in the oropharyngeal section. Oropharyngeal dysphagia is characterized by difficulty with the initiation of swallowing. Patients with esophageal dysphagia will thus most likely experience difficulty after the initiation of swallowing, while patients with oropharyngeal dysphagia will experience pain initiating swallowing.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: A patient presents to your clinic with dysphagia, odynophagia and acid reflux. A swallow test administered by a speech pathologist reveals the patient has difficulty and pain swallowing both solid and liquid food. Further investigation with high resolution esophageal manometry reveals low to no tonic contractions in the lower esophageal sphincter. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Difficulty swallowing liquids and solids suggest a motility issue over a mechanical issue that might come from a peptic structure or esophageal cancer. The high-resolution esophageal manometry scan measures pressure in the esophagus and acts as a surrogate to measure muscle contraction. The lack of muscle contraction suggests Scleroderma Esophagus where peristalsis does not occur, and the lower esophageal sphincter is perpetually open making the esophagus prone to acid reflux from the stomach. In distal esophageal spasm there is a simultaneous peristaltic contraction throughout the esophagus. Patients with a jackhammer esophagus often experience frequent and repetitive peristalsis movement in their esophagus.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.

preamble.title: Shared instructions
preamble.html:
Use the following stem to answer the next TWO Questions.

You are a third-year clerk interviewing a patient during your family medicine rotation. Mr.

Wiggum, a 53-year-old police officer, is concerned about some difficulty swallowing. He reports

that both foods and liquids feel like they get stuck in his chest, and that this has been fairly

constant over the past 4 years. Upon questioning, he admits that he rarely experiences associated

heartburn or chest pain, and that his symptoms are worse at night.

stem: Of these options, what is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Dysphagia of solids and liquids indicates a motility issue, and the onset of four years indicates a progressive nature. This could be scleroderma or achalasia. The patient reports no heartburn and nocturnal symptoms, characteristic of achalasia. Presence of heartburn could be achalasia or scleroderma.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which test would you order next to confirm Mr.Wiggum’s presumed diagnosis?

options.html: No other tests needed – can be diagnosed clinically

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Motility issues such as this (where both solids and liquids are affected) are best diagnosed with high resolution esophageal manometry. Mechanical issues (where solid foods only are affected) are best diagnosed with a barium swallow and X-ray, or endoscopy.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Adenocarcinoma of the esophagus is a complication of chronic GERD. Robert is a 59-yearold lawyer with recently diagnosed adenocarcinoma. Which treatment option is NOT an effective treatment for Robert’s esophageal adenocarcinoma?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Anti-reflux therapy is a treatment for GERD to prevent progression to Barrett’s esophagus and adenocarcinoma of the esophagus. Robert already has adenocarcinoma; antireflux therapy will not treat Robert’s cancer.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: A 5-year-old child is examined by their physician which reveals hepatomegaly. A request for initial imaging is made. You can immediately tell the child is very nervous at the prospect of imaging by their constant fidgeting. Which of the following initial imaging modalities are best suited to examine the child's liver?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Given the child’s young age, ionizing radiation should be avoided if possible as younger patients have increased life-long risk of developing cancer due to ionizing radiation exposure. This leaves MRIs and Ultrasounds. MRIs are rarely the first imaging modality used due to their cost and general lack of availability.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: A 45-year-old male presents to your clinic with severe abdominal pain. A supine abdominal CT is taken and shown below. Which of the following pathologies is most common given the patient’s imaging?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The small pockets of air in a line formation is the “String of pearls” sign which typically characterizes a small intestine issue such as small bowel obstruction. Large bowel obstruction and Colitis involve the large intestines. A foreign body would likely appear as a solid object (shown in white/grey).

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Giannina is a 25-year-old who is concerned about a progressively worse sense of constipation which is not relieved with over-the-counter laxatives. Her family physician suspects a bowel obstruction. Considering her presentation and age, what is the best imaging modality to confirm the diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Abdominal X-rays are effective in diagnosing bowel obstructions. A CT-scan would also confirm the diagnosis, but as a young patient, Giannina should avoid the large amounts of radiation from a CT scan.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Damian is a 27-year-old who presents to the emergency room with acute epigastric pain consistent with cholelithiasis (gallstones). Which imaging modality should the physician order to confirm the diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Ultrasound as an imaging modality is effective at diagnosing solid structures, such as gallstones. This imaging modality does not expose the patient to radiation.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Identify the structure of the GI tract that is properly matched with its arterial blood supply.
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The celiac trunk supplies the stomach, and proximal ⅓ of the duodenum (along with the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder). The superior mesenteric artery supplies the rest of the duodenum, jejunum, ilium, ascending colon, and transverse colon. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which statement on the development of the GI tract is true?

options.html: The proctodeum arises from the endoderm
The liver develops independently from the ventral mesentery and later connects to the midgut
The posterior side of the early embryological foregut eventually becomes the lesser curvature of the stomach
The trachea and the esophagus both develop from the foregut

answer:
The correct answer is D.

During week 4 of development, a tracheobronchial diverticulum forms, which eventually leads to the tracheal and esophagus. Option A is false - the proctodeum arises from the ectoderm. Option B is false - the liver buds out from the foregut when the embryological age is 3.5 weeks. Option C is also false - The posterior side of the foregut eventually becomes the greater curvature of the stomach.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: A surgeon is performing an appendectomy, which requires him to make an incision through the abdominal wall to remove the inflamed appendix. Which statement below is true?

options.html: The most superficial muscle layer is the external oblique, the middle muscle layer is the transverse abdominis, and the deepest muscle layer is the internal oblique.
An investing fascia surrounds each muscle layer of the abdominal wall.
The deep-most layer of the abdominal wall is the extraperitoneal fat layer.
Following the surgery, the surgeon will likely insert surgical sutures (stitches) in the Camper’s fascia.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Each abdominal wall muscle (external oblique, internal oblique, and transverse abdominis from most superficial to most deep) contains its own investing fascia. The deep-most layer of the anterior abdominal wall is the parietal peritoneum. Camper’s fascia is a superficial fatty layer that does not hold surgical sutures. The stitches were likely placed in the Scarpa’s fascia.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Choose the correct statement below pertaining to the rectus abdominis.

options.html: Superior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is enveloped by the internal obliques
Superior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is deep to the transverse abdominis.
Inferior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is enveloped by the external obliques.
Inferior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is deep to the transversalis fascia.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Superior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is found within the internal obliques. Inferior to the arcuate line, the rectus abdominis is deep to the transverse abdominis.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Either before or slightly after birth, the testes have reached their final location. Choose the one incorrect statement regarding descent of the testes.

options.html: The testes descend as a result of the gubernaculum shortening.
The spermatic cord contains the testicular artery, testicular vein, and the vas deferens
The layers surrounding the testes contain fascia originating from the external oblique, internal oblique, and transverse abdominis muscles
During descent, the testes pass through the inguinal canal.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

During the descent of the kidneys, the gubernaculum shortens, pulling the testes through the inguinal canal. In doing so, the testes are enveloped by the external oblique and internal oblique muscles, but not the transverse abdominis.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Choose the statement that correctly differentiates an indirect vs direct inguinal hernia.

options.html: Indirect hernias often pass into the scrotum, whereas direct hernias rarely do.
Direct hernias travel within the inguinal canal, whereas indirect hernias do not.
Direct hernias are more common than indirect hernias
Patients with a patent processus vaginalis are predisposed to direct hernias; patients with a weakness in the anterior abdominal wall are predisposed to indirect hernias.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

A is the only correct answer. Indirect hernias often pass into the scrotum of males or labium majus of females, via the inguinal canal. They are also more common than direct hernias, and patients with patent processes vaginalis are predisposed to indirect hernia

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which option correctly matches the artery in the foregut with the organ it supplies?

options.html: The left gastroepiploic artery supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach
The splenic artery supplies the spleen and the pancreas
The proper hepatic artery supplies the duodenum
The anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery supplies the gallbladder and liver

answer:
The correct answer is B.

The splenic artery branches from the celiac trunk and supplies the pancreas and spleen with oxygenated blood. The lesser curvature of the stomach receives blood from the gastric arteries. The proper hepatic artery supplies the liver, and the pancreaticoduodenal arteries supply the pancreas and the duodenum.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Select the statement that is true:

options.html: CCK is released by the pancreas in response to the presence of proteins and fat in the small intestine
Bile is secreted by gallbladder into the duodenum in order to emulsify fats and promote absorption through the enterocytes.
Histamine stimulates the release of gastrin by G cells and the secretion of acid by parietal cells
Acetylcholine released by the parasympathetic system provides positive stimulation to ECL cells, Gastrin cells, D cells and parietal cells.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

CCK is secreted by duodenal cells in response to the presence of proteins and fats in the small intestine and has the additional functions of delaying gastric emptying and stimulating gall bladder contractions. Gastrin stimulates the release of Histamine by ECL cells and the release of acid by parietal cells. Acetylcholine inhibits D cells and their secretion of somatostatin, which plays a role in reducing stomach acidity.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: During a severe H. pylori infection of the antrum of the stomach, many of the D cells die off. Which of the following symptoms may be observed in a patient with a severe H. pylori infection?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The D cells produce somatostatin, which is primarily released when the stomach contents reach a pH below 3.0, and they have an inhibitory paracrine effect on G cells, ECL cells, and parietal cells to reduce the overall acidity of the stomach. In the absence of somatostatin, the increasing acidity can degrade the epithelial lining of the stomach and lead to ulceration.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: A patient presents to your family clinic concerned about their persistent heartburn for the past two months. Which observation allows for a positive diagnosis of GERD?

options.html: A patient’s heartburn is not relieved by antacids or PPIs
An endoscopy does not show signs of erosion in the patient’s esophagus
A 24-hr ambulatory pH monitoring of the patient’s esophagus indicating persistent pH values of 4 or less
A patient points to the center of their chest and claims there’s a burning sensation

answer:
The correct answer is C.

This 24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring showing esophageal pH below 4 indicates gastric acid entering the esophagus (although it would typically be used by patients who have failed a PPI trial). GERD can be erosive; however, 70% of GERD cases are nonerosive. Ordinarily, GERD is confirmed based on symptoms and positive response to a PPI trial.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following options would NOT be part of a potential management plan for a patient with chronic GERD?

options.html: Alcohol and smoking cessation, diet modification

answer:
The correct answer is D.

In GERD, stomach acid travels superiorly from the stomach to the esophagus, in part because of a dilated lower-esophageal sphincter. Dilatating the esophageal sphincter would exacerbate the patient’s symptoms of GERD.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: Which of the following signs and symptoms would be the largest concern for malignancy in a patient with a gastric ulcer?

options.html: A biopsy of the ulcer reveals a round, flat and “punched out” ulcerating region of the stomach
A biopsy reveals the ulcer has raised edges and is an oval appearance
Microscopic analysis of the tissue reveals erosion of the submucosa and the muscularis mucosa as well
The patient experiences symptoms of hemorrhage, regurgitation and radiating back pain

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Some gastric ulcers may be ulcerating cancers. An endoscopy of the ulcer that reveals an oval appearance, with irregular edges, raised edges, and gastric folds that don’t radiate to the edge indicates an ulcerating cancer. An ulcer erodes the submucosa layer as well as the muscularis mucosa layer. The complications of peptic ulcers include hemorrhage, regurgitation, obstruction and radiating back pain.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: A 65-year-old patient arrives at your clinic with complaints of heartburn and regurgitation. He states this occurs very intermittently (perhaps once every month), and only after eating a very large meal. The patient currently takes many medications on a daily basis and expresses a strong preference against adding any more regular medications to his routine. The patient has a habit of routinely forgetting to take his medication for sometimes days at a time. Which of the following medications would you likely prescribe this patient for his intermittent GERD?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Antacids are likely the best choice for this patient. Antacids are fast acting and provide symptomatic relief, used in uncomplicated symptoms. Proton pump inhibitors and H2 receptor antagonists would likely need to be included into his regular routine which is not ideal if the patient is only intermittently experiencing symptoms. Furthermore, with H2 receptor antagonists and PPIs patients can experience tachyphylaxis or a rebound effect (from the built-up gastrin) respectively if the patient skips doses.

lectureMeta: The student-written bank the Class of 2024 Academic Directors built in May 2021 and the Meds 2025 volunteers re-filed week by week. About half the cardiology questions and a handful of the respirology ones were reviewed by faculty; the rest were not.
stem: You are treating a patient with a gastric ulcer. In your investigations to determine the cause of the ulcer you take a brief history which reveals no significant finds other than Warfarin and NSAIDs medication use. A serology test for H. pylori comes back positive, and a C13 Urea Breath Test comes back negative. Based on your investigations, which of the following treatment recommendations do you recommend? Select TWO correct answers.

options.html: Prescribe amoxicillin for H. pylori infection
Prescribe tetracycline for H. pylori infection

answer:
The correct answer is B, C.

Gastric ulcers are commonly caused by NSAID use whereas duodenal ulcers are commonly caused by H. pylori infections. This is further confirmed by the C13 Urea Breath test to determine if there is an active H. pylori infection, the positive serology test indicates that the patient has had H. pylori in the past, but not necessarily currently. A proton pump inhibitor is an appropriate treatment recommendation for both gastric and duodenal ulcers.

stem: Regis visited an urgent care clinic worried about possible stomach cancer. For the past two months, he’s had intense upper abdominal pain after eating, and when he was sick with the flu last week, he noticed that his vomit had blood in it. An endoscopy was requisitioned, and the following was observed in his pyloric antrum. What is Regis’s most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The question stem indicates that the lesion was observed in the pyloric antrum (or in the stomach). Based on the flat, “punched out” appearance, this would likely be a benign gastric ulcer. Note, this is not an erosion as it is clearly a complete breach in the mucosa. Erosions are lesions which are less deep.

stem: There are several classes of drugs that are used to reduce the acidity in the stomach. Which statement below is true?

options.html: Antacids are safe for long-term use with minimal side effects or adverse drug reactions
Prostaglandins reduce the acidity in the stomach by inhibiting proton pumps in the mucosa
H2 receptor antagonists are the most appropriate prescription for the elderly population
PPIs irreversibly inhibit active transport of protons into the lumen of the stomach

answer:
The correct answer is D.

This is the mechanism of action of PPIs. Antacids can have many side effects depending on their composition, from diarrhea to constipation, to drug-drug interactions, etc. Prostaglandins increase the amount of mucus present, protecting the mucosa from stomach acid. H2 receptor antagonists should be prescribed with caution in the elderly population.

stem: For a patient with idiopathic gastroparesis leading to chronic nausea and vomiting, which option below would NOT be a suitable recommendation for treatment?

options.html: Have more frequent, but smaller meals
Reduce pop and alcohol in the diet
Avoid the use of antiemetic drugs due to the rebound effect

answer:
The correct answer is C.

For patients with gastroparesis, the patient should be educated on having smaller, more frequent meals, reducing pop and alcohol, ceasing smoking, maintaining tight sugar control. To treat the associated symptoms of nausea, antiemetics are prescribed.

stem: Eight weeks ago, Regis was diagnosed with a gastric ulcer. Since then, he has been taking his antibiotic medications to treat the underlying bacterial cause. Today, you are working for a gastroenterologist who has asked you to perform a test to confirm that all of the bacteria has been eradicated. Which test result would indicate an abated infection and would fit with Regis’s history?

options.html: Negative H. pylori IgG serology test

answer:
The correct answer is B.

If Regis had an ulcer caused by H. pylori, even if the bacteria was eradicated, the H. pylori IgG serology test would be positive. Rather, to confirm eradication of the bacterial, a urease breath test should be performed. If negative, it means the infection has subsided.

stem: 54-year-old Taylor arrives at your clinic. She describes how she recently started playing spike ball and has been enjoying it, but this activity is always accompanied by feelings of nausea. Further history leads the physician to suspect motion sickness. Which of the following medications would be most appropriate for Taylor?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Antihistamines (Histamine H1 antagonists) are primarily useful for motion sickness as they act on the vestibular afferents and within the brainstem. 5HT3 receptor antagonists are primarilyused for chemotherapy-induced nausea and post-operative nausea. D2 antagonists are primarily used for nausea induced by toxins and migraine/opioid induced nausea. Cannabinoids are indicated for chemotherapy induced nausea when other agents aren’t working.

stem: A patient arrives at your clinic with concerns of chronic nausea over a period of at least two years. The patient reports this typically occurs after a meal, and often he can’t even finish eating the meal despite what he’s eating. The physician has a strong suspicion for gastroparesis. Which of the following findings would be in line with the physician’s suspected diagnosis?

options.html: An abdominal CT scan showing narrowing at the pyloric sphincter
A gastric emptying study showing delayed gastric emptying at the 4-hour mark

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Gastroparesis is objectively delayed gastric emptying in the absence of a mechanical obstruction. A positive secession splash sign is where the physician listens with their stethoscope to the patient’s belly, and the splashing can indicate signs of obstruction. Cannabis history may be useful in the diagnosis of cannabinoid hyperemesis. An abdominal CT scan showing a mechanical obstruction would point away from the diagnosis of gastroparesis. A gastric emptying study showing severely delayed gastric emptying would be in line with a diagnosis of gastroparesis.

stem: Which of the following enzymes are responsible for the breakdown of disaccharides into monosaccharaides?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Brush-border enzymes break down disaccharides into monosaccharides. Salivary amylase is secreted in the mouth and breakdown starch into oligosaccharides. At the level of the small intestine pancreatic amylase breaks down oligosaccharides into disaccharides.

stem: Five years ago, Gerry had an operation to remove a large portion of his ileum. What are some expected sequelae to this surgical resection? Select all that apply.

options.html: Increased polysaccharide content in the stool

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum, along with other fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) and Vitamin B12. With a resected ileum, Gerry will have reduced bile salt reabsorption, and consequently, fatty stool, called steatorrhea.

stem: Several enzymes are responsible for digesting proteins consumed in the diet. Which statement below is true?

options.html: Pepsinogen is secreted by the salivary glands to breakdown oligopeptides
The pancreas secretes trypsin via endocrine mechanisms
Proteins must be broken down into single amino acids to be absorbed
Nine amino acids must be consumed in the diet and cannot be synthesized in the body

answer:
The correct answer is D.

There are nine essential amino acids that the human body cannot synthesize endogenously and must be consumed. Salivary glands secrete salivary amylase to break down oligosaccharides. The pancreas has exocrine and endocrine functions - secretion of trypsinogen occurs via exocrine functions. Lastly, amino acids, dipeptides, and tripeptides are absorbed by the small intestine, where cellular proteases can further digest these into single amino acids.

stem: Which of the following signs/symptoms would you NOT expect to find in a patient with Celiac Disease?

options.html: A duodenal biopsy displaying blunted villi
A duodenal biopsy showing increased inflammation of the bowel
A blood test confirming a deficiency in pancreatic enzymes
HLA typing indicating the patient is positive for HLA-DQ2

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Celiac disease is a malabsorption disease that is due to pathological changes in the mucosal surface of the intestine from an allergic inflammatory reaction to gluten. Thus, a duodenal biopsy may show blunted villi and increased inflammation of the bowels. 95% of patients are positive for HLA DQ2, however this is also fairly prevalent in the general population as well. Patients with Celiac disease may also have a skin rash – dermatitis herpetiformis.

stem: A patient presents to your clinic with a 3-month history of Diarrhea. They describe their stool as large in volume and watery, but not urgent and a normal frequency (2 times per day). The patient does not report any previous infections in the past year and is not taking any medications. The patient however reports feeling of fatigue and weight loss despite his eating habits not changing. Furthermore, a blood test confirms the patient had multiple vitamin deficiencies. Which of the following classifications of the patient’s diarrhea is most accurate?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The patient’s symptoms have been lasting longer than 4 weeks which suggest a more chronic presentation. Furthermore, the large volume of stool but infrequent and non-urgent presentation signify a small bowel pathology as opposed to a large bowel disorder. The deficiency in vitamins and weight loss suggest a malabsorption/maldigestion issue where the food/vitamins are passed into the bowels and water follows the food content into the bowel creating a watery diarrhea.

stem: At a yearly check-up a patient commented that many of her long-standing dietary issues were resolved after she started avoiding carbohydrates and gluten. For example, bloating and diarrhea stopped after she cut out gluten 4 months ago. For peace of mind, she requests a formal diagnosis of celiac disease – what is the next test that you order?

options.html: Serology testing for tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibody only
Serology testing for tissue transglutaminase antibody plus IgA levels
Serology testing for IgA levels only
Genetic testing for HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8

answer:
The correct answer is D.

For patients who are currently gluten-free, TTG and IgA levels will not help in elucidating a diagnosis. Gluten-free patients require genetic testing for the human leukocyte antigens HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. If the patient had recently had gluten in his or her diet, a physician may request serology testing for TTG antibody plus IgA levels. Note that if the TTG antibody levels are low and the IgA levels are low, it’s non-diagnostic.

stem: Which of the following treatment strategies is generally indicated in most cases of infectious diarrhea?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Aggressive oral hydration is generally indicated in most cases of infectious diarrhea (inflammatory and non-inflammatory) as large volumes of water are lost from the body. Nutrient supplementation may only be appropriate in patients with a malabsorption cause for diarrhea, requiring additional supplements. Antibiotics are not required for most infectious agents causing diarrhea. Antimotility agents are contraindicated in patients with bloody stool or if C. difficile is a consideration, as this can lead to toxic megacolon.

stem: Alejandro came to the emergency department with acute diarrhea, that began shortly after a barbecue yesterday. He’s worried that he caught food poisoning from some uncooked beef. As the resident emergency doctor, which is NOT one of your next actions?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

In this presentation, the clinical suspicion for an E. coli infection is high, particularly due to the risk of eating uncooked beef. In such cases, antibiotics should be avoided, as this can exacerbate hemolytic uremic syndrome.

stem: A patient presents with bloody diarrhea following a 2-week course of clindamycin to treat bacterial pneumonia. A stool culture tests positive for C. difficile. She is 34 years old and is stable. What are the next steps for this patient?

options.html: Prescribe vancomycin for the C. difficile infection
Admit to the hospital, refer to gastroenterologist
Refer to surgery for resection of the offending area

answer:
The correct answer is B.

For C. difficile infections, vancomycin is a good empiric therapy. C. difficile infections are often the result of an antibiotic course of clindamycin. A gastroenterologist may be consulted; however the patient should receive antibiotics for the C. difficile infection immediately.

stem: Which of the following patients with a history of constipation would NOT be indicated for a colonoscopy?

options.html: A 35-year-old patient with unexplained weight loss

answer:
The correct answer is C.

A colonoscopy for the investigation of constipation should be avoided in patients under the age of 50, unless the patient has red flags such as bloody stool, anemia, weight loss, sudden change in bowel habits or a familiar history of colon cancer.

stem: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate first-line treatment option for a patient with constipation?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Docusate is stool softener that is generally not recommended due to the lack of evidence for its efficacy. There is low quality evidence for increasing dietary intake and it’s an inexpensive option for many patients. PEG3350 and Lactulose (not PEGLYTE) are both osmotic laxatives used as front-line treatment.

stem: Larry is a 45-year-old who has complaints of constipation. He describes his bowel movements as about once every two days, and nearly all of these require straining. His stool is described as hard and lumpy. He stays hydrated but has a lot of processed foods. His physical exam is relatively unremarkable except reduced bowel sounds. Preliminary blood work is also unremarkable. Based on this presentation, what is the next best recommended treatment for Larry? Choose the best two answers.
answer:
The correct answer is C, E.

Fiber is a good first-line treatment for constipation; patients should be advised to slowly increase fiber in their diet to about 20-30g per day. PEG3350 is an osmotic laxative that retains fluids in the colon and softens stools. Given the lack of any red flags, colonoscopy, defecating proctogram, and anorectal manometry are not indicated.

stem: Which of the following drugs is NOT appropriate to prescribe for a patient with constipation?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Delta opioid receptor agonists is an anti-diarrheal drug which plays a large role in inhibiting motility which could further worsen motility in a patient with constipation.

stem: Archie is a 43-year-old who arrived at his family doctor seeking medications for his ongoing diarrhea. A gastrointestinal infection has already been ruled out. Archie has a past medical history of narcotic abuse, for which he is currently in recovery. He also takes medications throughout the day to manage his bipolarism. Which medication would you recommend? Select TWO answers.

options.html: None – advise Archie to drink less water

answer:
The correct answer is D, G.

Diarrhea is rarely caused by too much water consumption, so A is not correct. Domperidone and Erythromycin are prokinetics - these would not help the diarrhea but make it worse! Both loperamide and diphenoxylate are opioid antagonists, but diphenoxylate has abuse potential and should be avoided with Archie’s history of narcotic abuse. Cholestyramine is a bile-salt binding resin and would treat the diarrhea; however, this could also cause a negative drug-drug interaction with medication for Archie’s bipolarism. PeptoBismol is generally recognized as safe for most individuals (in rare cases results in neurotoxicity).

stem: You suspect one of your patients has irritable bowel syndrome. Which of the following initial investigations is NOT appropriate for this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The IgG Food sensitivity test has been widely debunked and should not part of the diagnostic workup for a patient with suspected IBS. IgG production is a normal immune response to food. A fecal Occult Blood stool test can be used to detect the microscopic presence of blood in stool. IBS can have a dramatic impact on the patient’s mental wellness and this should always be a consideration. In patients with red flags (over 50, dysphagia and a history of colon cancer) a colonoscopy can be offered to assess underlying pathologies.

stem: Which of the following signs/symptoms in a patient is necessary for the diagnosis of functional dyspepsia?

options.html: Pain in the upper part of the abdomen (epigastric pain)

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Functional Dyspepsia is dyspepsia (pain in the upper abdomen) with no evidence of organic disease. Patients can present with postprandial fullness, early satiety, epigastric pain or burning, however all pains must have a negative endoscopy excluding any structural diseases to explain the symptoms.

stem: Which patient below satisfies the Rome IV criteria for irritable bowel syndrome?

options.html: Anthony, who has had two months of abdominal pain associated with defecation with an increase in stool frequency
Bertha, who has had constipation about twice per week, and has 6 months of continuous abdominal pain regardless of her state of constipation
Christopher, who for the past six months has had unbearably painful bowel movements and has noticed streaks of blood upon wiping.

answer:
The correct answer is E.

For IBS according to the Rome IV Criteria, a patient requires having three months of recurrent abdominal pain, and two of: 1) the abdominal pain is related to defecation; 2) a change in stool frequency; and 3) a change in stool appearance. Anthony’s symptoms have not lasted long enough. Bertha’s abdominal pain does not seem to be related to defecation. Christopher’s presentation is more consistent with constipation and hemorrhoids, but not IBS.

stem: You are a rural family doctor seeing a new patient, Eric, who has recently moved to your small town in Northern Ontario. Shortly before Eric moved, he was diagnosed with dyspepsia but was unable to discuss treatment options. Which options below would NOT be appropriate for Eric’s management for dyspepsia?

options.html: Consider antibiotics to treat a possible H. pylori infection
Council the patient on diet modification
Council the patient on exercise reduction to reduce exacerbation of symptoms
Assess Eric’s psychosocial status and consider prescribing antidepressants

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Non-pharmacological treatments of dyspepsia can include lifestyle changes such as improving one’s diet and increasing exercise. Dyspepsia can be caused by an H. pylori infection or by psychosocial factors: antibiotics or antidepressants may be valuable depending on the underlying cause of Eric’s dyspepsia.

stem: A patient arrives at your clinic with concerns of dysphagia, fatigue and weight loss. The patient has previously been diagnosed with GERD. After a thorough history and physical this prompts investigation with endoscopy which reveals an abnormality in the lining of the distal esophagus. Which of the following cancerous tissues is most likely?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Esophageal neoplasms tend to be mostly adenocarcinomas in the west. It’s possible the patient’s GERD may have led to metaplasia of the distal esophageal tissue (Barrett’s esophagus) which may have developed into an adenocarcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma which is found in the esophagus tends to present in the mid-esophageal region.

stem: A 50-year-old patient presents to your clinic for a colonoscopy after concerns for rectal bleeding and alternating diarrhea and constipation. Lesions were found on the descending colon. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.html: The lesions were likely colorectal polyps and treatment involves surgical removal
The lesions were likely colorectal polyps and treatment involves medical therapy
The lesions were likely serrated adenomas and treatment involves surgical removal
The lesions were likely serrated adenomas and treatment involves medical therapy

answer:
The correct answer is A.

These lesions are likely colorectal polyps as serrated adenomas tend to be more common on the right side (ascending colon). Colorectal cancer is largely preventable through early screening and treatment involves surgical removal of the polyps.

stem: A 50-year-old patient with chronic GERD is struggling to afford his pantoprazole prescription and asks you if there will be long tern complications if he doesn’t take his medication. What do you say to him?

options.html: No, you may have long-term epigastric discomfort but will otherwise be fine.
Chronic GERD could lead to Barrett’s esophagus, which can lead to esophageal cancer.
Chronic GERD could lead to adenocarcinoma, which could lead to Barrett’s esophagus.
Chronic GERD could lead to irritable bowel syndrome if left unchecked.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

GERD can have very severe consequences if untreated, including esophageal cancer (adenocarcinoma). If he cannot afford pantoprazole, perhaps there is a cheaper PPI available that would help with his symptoms, or perhaps the patient qualifies for social supports to help fund this medication.

stem: Chadwick Boseman was an American actor who played King T’Challa in Marvel’s Black Panther. In 2020, at the age of 43, Boseman passed away from stage 4 colon cancer. Which statement regarding colon cancer is true?

options.html: Stage 4 indicates that the cancer has spread to the fat surrounding the colon but not yet the serosa
Colorectal cancers most commonly arise from colitis, although colorectal polyps can also cause colorectal cancers
“Right-sided” colon cancer presents with rectal bleeding and a mass on digital rectal exam
Diagnosis can be made with colonoscopy and biopsy but staging requires X-ray and CT of the chest and abdomen

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Stage 4 colorectal cancer indicates that the cancer has spread to the serosa. Almost all colorectal cancers arise from polyps. Lastly, left-sided colorectal cancer presents with rectal bleeding and a mass on DRE, whereas right-sided colorectal cancer presents with anemia and weight loss.

stem: Which of the following features is NOT a characteristic of ulcerative colitis?

options.html: Inflammation at the level of the mucosa

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Ulcerative Colitis is characterized by lesions which begin at the rectum and extend to the proximal end of the bowel. Patchy skip lesions occur intermittently throughout the colon.

stem: Which of the following treatments is the best intervention for colonic stricture resulting from Crohn's Disease?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Endoscopic balloon dilation is the most common treatment for colonic strictures, to dilate the colon. Patient’s may have to do this routinely. Surgical resections are only indicated in the most severe cases due to the risk of contributing to malabsorption.

stem: A patient with a 3-week history of bloody diarrhea presents to your clinic. The physician suspects the patient has Ulcerative Colitis and is starting their diagnostic workup. Which of the following is not an appropriate initial investigation for the workup of Ulcerative Colitis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Ulcerative Colitis is characterized by lesions that begin at the rectum and extend proximally, thus as an initial investigation only a sigmoidoscopy may be recommended. A colonoscopy is associated with greater risks and is generally done at a later stage to determine the extent of the colon involved. A stool culture and sensitivity test is appropriate in this scenario to rule out any potential infection. A fecal Calprotectin test may also be appropriate to measure the amount of gut inflammation and this can be tracked overtime.

stem: Ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn’s disease (DC) are two forms of inflammatory bowel disease. Which statement below is true?

options.html: CD is more likely to be continuous whereas UC is patchy.
UC occurs mainly in the left large bowel; CD occurs mainly in the right large bowel.
Fecal calprotectin will be elevated in patients with UC but not with CD.
None of the above statements are true

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Ulcerative colitis is a continuous inflammation of the large bowel Crohn’s disease is a discontinuous inflammation of the entire GI tract (“gum-to-bum”). Both are inflammatory diseases, and blood tests for both will indicate elevated fecal calprotectin. None of the answers are true statements.

stem: A patient presents to his family doctor with left lower quadrant abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Suspecting inflammatory bowel disease, the physician orders a colonoscopy and biopsy of the various locations in the large intestine. Which statement of the pathology report or colonoscopy report is most suggestive of a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis?

options.html: Pathology report: “There is abnormal mucosal physiology of the ascending colon but normal mucosal physiology of the descending colon.”
Pathology report: “Hematoxylin and eosin stain of the tissue sample indicates the presence of granulomas in the mucosa.”
Colonoscopy report: “Shallow ulcers line the descending colon leading to the presence of pseudo-polyps.”
Colonoscopy report: “The inflamed area is patchy and discontinuous.”

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Ulcerative colitis is a continuous inflammation of the large bowel, beginning at the rectum and spreading proximally up the GI tract - if this was UC and there was abnormal physiology in the ascending colon, there would need to be abnormal physiology in the descending colon, so options A and D are false. Granulomas are characteristic of Crohn’s disease, not ulcerative colitis, so option B is false. Ulcerative colitis is associated with shallow ulcers, whereas Crohn’s disease is associated with fissuring ulcers.

stem: Ryan was recently diagnosed with mild Crohn’s disease. Which treatment option is most appropriate for Ryan?

options.html: Ryan should avoid grain and gluten products
Ryan should be prescribed budesonide or ASA
Ryan should undergo endoscopic balloon dilatation
Ryan should undergo surgical resection of the affected area

answer:
The correct answer is B.

For a mild case, Ryan can be prescribed weak anti-inflammatory drugs such as budesonide or ASA. In more severe cases, Ryan may be prescribed prednisone or biological agents. In more severe cases, balloon dilatation or surgical resection could also be warranted.

stem: A patient presents to your clinic with rectal bleeding that has been ongoing for the past two days. An initial history shows that the patient has been losing a significant amount of blood over the past few days and a CBC shows the patient has become anemic. Which of the following interventional strategies is appropriate?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

During an angiogram a catheter is guided into the mesenteric arteries and contrast is injected to examine the location of bleeding. The angiogram also offers therapeutic potential in circumstances where the patient’s vitals are unstable – the site of the blood site can be determined and therapeutically embolized. An RBC scan or colonoscopy is typically referred for patients who are more stable. An endoscopy is not appropriate for a lower GI bleed.

stem: Which statement below on gastrointestinal bleeding is correct?

options.html: Upper GI bleeds present with melena, whereas lower GI bleeds present with hematochezia
The first step in the management for a patient with GI bleeding is to perform an endoscopy and colonoscopy
Upper GI bleeds occur proximal to the jejunal-ileal junction, whereas lower GI bleeds occur distal to the jejunal-ileal junction
The location of GI bleeding can be deduced at any point in the GI tract via endoscopy or colonoscopy

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Melena (black, tarry stool) is characteristic of an upper GI bleed, occurring proximal to the ligament of Treitz (duodenal-jejunal junction). However, hematochezia (bright red or maroon-colored blood) is characteristic of a lower GI bleed. The first step in any patient with GI bleeding is to assess the patient’s stability and vitals. Note, for the GI bleeding, there are some regions that can’t be reached by endoscopic methods. GI bleeds in these areas are called obscure bleeding.
