stem: A patient has presented to the emergency room feeling faint after vomiting blood. What is the most effective treatment for the patient if it is determined that he has ruptured esophageal varices?

options.html: Pantoloc (PPI), Octreotide and Antibiotic medication followed by an endoscopy
Endoscopy positive for esophageal varices followed by Pantoloc (PPI), Octreotide medication
Endoscopy positive for esophageal varices followed by Band ligation
Pantoloc, Octreotide medication followed by colonoscopy

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The patient’s symptoms, hematemesis and the elevated BUN/creatinine ratio suggest an upper GI bleed. Esophageal variceal bleeding is an urgent condition. The proton pump inhibitors decrease fibrinolysis and stabilize platelet plugs; Octreotide decrease portal flow from the liver; and the antibiotics have been shown to reduce mortality in patients with upper GI bleed with liver cirrhosis.

stem: Which of the following options best describes the features of the jejunum?

options.html: Long vasa recta, few arcades with large loops
Long vasa recta, many arcades with short loops
Short vasa recta, few arcades with large loops
Short vasa recta, many arcades with short loops

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The jejunum’s blood supply can be characterized by long vasa recta followed by a few arcades with large loops. The ileum’s blood supply contains short vasa recta with many arcades with short loops.

stem: Which of the following symptoms regarding hemorrhoid are true?

options.html: Patients are likely to notice internal and external hemorrhoid as they’re both painful
Patients are likely to report external hemorrhoid as they can feel it but both internal and external hemorrhoid are painless
Both internal and external hemorrhoid can be associated with blood loss and are both painful
Both internal and external hemorrhoid are associated with blood loss but only external hemorrhoid are painful

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Internal and external hemorrhoids are both characterized by a thrombus of venous circulation that either occur at the anal opening (external hemorrhoids) or occur inside the anus above the pectinate line (internal hemorrhoids). Due to the location of the internal hemorrhoids and their lack of innervation by somatic sensory fibers, they are not painful, while external hemorrhoids are. Both internal and external hemorrhoids are prone to bleeding.

stem: Which of the following methods can be used to correctly differentiate the ileum and jejunum in a cadaver lab?

options.html: The jejunum receives its blood supply from the superior mesenteric artery, whereas the ileum receives its blood supply from the inferior mesenteric artery
The jejunum has more mesenteric fat than the ileum
The jejunum has longer vasa recta and larger Arcades loops
The jejunum is the location of Meckel’s diverticulum
The jejunum is peritoneal whereas the ileum is retroperitoneal

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The jejunum and ileum both receive their blood supply from the superior mesenteric artery. The ileum has more mesenteric fat than the jejunum. Meckel’s diverticulum occurs in the ileum, about 2-feet proximal to the ileal-cecal junction. Both the jejunum and ileum are peritoneal. The jejunum has less mesenteric fat relative to the ileum.

stem: A patient has a complete occlusion of their right colic artery, an artery that supplies blood to part of the large intestine. Which statement is true?

options.html: The patient is highly at risk of developing ischemic bowel syndrome
The patient will require endovascular surgery to restore blood flow to the transverse colon
The patient’s ascending colon will be supplied fresh blood by the middle colic artery and the marginal artery
The life-threatening condition requires immediate colectomy

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The arteries that supply the large intestine anastomose at the marginal artery (of Drummond). If the right colic artery was occluded, the ascending colon would receive blood from other colic arteries.

stem: A. patient presents to his family doctor with constipation and an associated painful anal sphincter. Upon wiping, there are streaks of bright red blood. What type of hemorrhoid would lead to this presentation and why?

options.html: Internal hemorrhoids, because of the presence of pain
External hemorrhoids, because these are innervated by visceral sensory fibers
Internal hemorrhoids, because the blood is bright red instead of dark red
External hemorrhoids, because of their presence below the pectinate line

answer:
The correct answer is D.

External hemorrhoids are hemorrhoids situated below the pectinate line. These are innervated by somatic sensory fibers and a patient with external hemorrhoids will feel pain.

stem: John is a 56-year-old man, who presents to his family doctor with concerns about colon cancer. He doesn’t report any symptoms and appears to be very healthy, but he started to worry incessantly after his brother was recently diagnosed with colon cancer. John has never had any screening for colorectal cancer in the past. Which of the following tests is most appropriate?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

John is at a greater risk for colorectal cancer than the average population due to a firstdegree relative having colon cancer. John should be referred to do a colonoscopy (the “gold standard”) as opposed to a FIT test which the average risk patient does.

stem: Which of the following options regarding colorectal screening is correct?

options.html: Colonoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy both require sedation and intensive preparation
Patients who screen positive on a flexible sigmoidoscopy require a follow-up colonoscopy
The feces sample from a FIT test primarily looks for microscopic cancerous tissue
Average risk patients above the age of 50 are offered a colonoscopy every 2 years

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy requires significantly less preparation (an enema the morning of and no sedation) relative to a colonoscopy. Patients who screen positive on a FS must do a colonoscopy to remove all polyps in the distal parts of the colon, which the FS cannot reach. The FIT sample primarily looks for microscopic heme, to detect occult bleeding which can signify the presence of polyps in the colon. Average risk patients above the age of 50 are offered a colonoscopy every 10 years.

stem: Marc is a 44-year-old patient from northern Ontario. As part of your family medicine residency, you are performing a rotation in Marc’s isolated town. You learn from Marc that his father died of colorectal cancer at the age of 53. His health history is highly suggestive of Crohn’s disease lasting several years, and you are awaiting for some bloodwork to confirm the diagnosis. Given Marc’s family history and positive diagnosis of Crohn’s, what will you recommend for Marc in terms of screening for colorectal cancer?

options.html: Marc should perform a FIT test every two years once he turns 50.
Marc should undergo a colonoscopy test every five years effective immediately
Marc should undergo a colonoscopy test every two years effective immediately.
Marc should undergo a colonoscopy test every two years that include biopsies effective immediately

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Marc would be considered high risk for colorectal cancer with a first-degree family member having had colorectal cancer. His screening should involve a colonoscopy every two years, with occasional biopsies, beginning ten years earlier than the age of diagnosis of his family member. For low-risk patients, a FIT test every two years is acceptable. For medium-risk patients, the patient should receive a colonoscopy every five years.

stem: Which of the following options describes the blood supply and structure of a hepatic lobule?

options.html: The center of each lobule contains a branch of the hepatic bile duct, hepatic portal vein and hepatic artery, while each corner of the lobule contains a branch of the hepatic vein
The center of each lobule contains a branch of the hepatic artery, while each corner of the lobule contains a branch of the bile duct, hepatic portal vein and hepatic vein
The center of each lobule contains a branch of the hepatic vein, while each corner of the lobule contains a branch of the bile duct, hepatic portal vein and hepatic artery
The center of each lobule contains a branch of the hepatic vein and hepatic portal vein, while each corner of the lobule contains a branch of the bile duct and hepatic artery

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Each hepatic lobule is roughly hexagonal in shape. The corners of the lobule contain a branch of the hepatic artery, hepatic portal vein and bile duct, while the center of the lobule contains the hepatic vein.

stem: In portal hypertension large volumes of venous blood flow through the portal-caval anastomoses in other sites of the body to enter systemic circulation, leading to the development of varicose veins and other site-specific pathologies. Which of the following pathologies are you NOT likely to see in a patient with portal hypertension? Select two options.
answer:
The correct answer is B, E.

External hemorrhoids are not likely because the venous blood supply for this region (below the pectinate line) does not course through the portal system. Internal hemorrhoids however can develop due to the portal-caval system that drains blood form this region. Moreover, the paraumbilical veins and the esophageal veins are also likely to experience pathologies (varicose veins) due to the portal caval anastomoses in the region. Rightventricular hypertrophy is not a complication of portal hypertension, but perhaps a cause of it.

stem: A surgeon is trying to clamp the most proximal portion of the artery that supplies the gallbladder. Where should the physician look to clamp this artery?

options.html: Inside the triangle of Calot, along the hepatic artery
At the porta hepatis at the common hepatic artery
At the porta hepatis at the proper hepatic artery
At hepatoduodenal ligament at the proper hepatic artery

answer:
The correct answer is A.

The cystic artery (stems of the right hepatic artery) and lies within the triangle of Calot. The borders of the triangle of Calot are the liver, the cystic duct, and the common hepatic duct.

stem: The gallbladder’s purpose is to both store and concentrate bile. Beginning in the gallbladder, what is the order of structures that bile passes through before entering the duodenum?

options.html: Cystic duct -> common bile duct -> common hepatic duct -> sphincter of Oddi
Common bile duct -> cystic duct -> common hepatic duct -> sphincter of Oddi
Cystic duct -> common bile duct -> pancreatic duct -> sphincter of Oddi
Cystic duct -> common hepatic duct -> pancreatic duct -> ampulla of Vater

answer:
The correct answer is C.

From the gallbladder, bile traverses the cystic duct followed by the common bile duct. The common bile duct meets with the pancreatic duct, and bile is secreted into the duodenum through the ampulla of Vater. The rate of secretion is controlled by the sphincter of Oddi.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Ultrasound is the initial modality of choice in patients with suspected biliary tract obstructions. CT and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is contraindicated in pregnant patients.

Confirm there is no Acute Liver Failure and reassure patient

The correct answer is A.

stem: Choose the three correct statements pertaining to liver failure.

In a patient with liver failure, albumin is decreased
In a patient with liver failure, bilirubin is increased
In a patient with liver failure, bilirubin is decreased
In a patient with liver failure, INR/PT is increased
In a patient with liver failure, INR/PT is decreased

answer:
The correct answer is B, C, E.

Decreased albumin, increased bilirubin, and increased INR/PT are indications of chronic liver disease and liver failure. The liver is responsible for the production of many plasma proteins (primarily Albumin), hepatic clearance of Bilirubin and the production of several coagulation factors.

stem: A 36-year-old patient presents with epigastric pain that radiates to his back. The pain started two months ago. The patient has a history of regular alcohol use (>3 drinks per day) and admits to eating a bit too much fast food. The patient’s blood tests return show elevated ALP and GGT, but normal levels of AST, ALT, albumin, bilirubin, and a normal PT/INR. Based on this presentation, which of these conditions is most likely?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GTT) are liver enzymes specific to the bile ducts. Of the four options, cholelithiasis is the most likely based on these test results and presentation. It is worth noting that the patient could also have any cholestatic disease and more tests would be necessary to come to a firm diagnosis (such as an abdominal ultrasound to confirm the presence of gallstones).

stem: A patient comes to your clinic with a fever, general malaise and pain in their upper abdomen that has lasted the past 2 days. The patient describes the onset of symptoms after having sex with a new partner who has Hepatitis A. Which of the following tests should the patient order, and if it comes back positive, what is the likely prognosis?

options.html: Hepatitis A IgG test, this will likely not lead to a chronic hepatitis
Hepatitis A IgG test, this will likely lead to a chronic hepatitis
Hepatitis A IgM test, this will likely not lead to a chronic hepatitis
Hepatitis A IgM test, this will likely lead to a chronic hepatitis

answer:
The correct answer is C.

The physician should order Hepatitis A IgM levels, as these antibodies are synthesized in the early stages of an infection. IgG antibodies are synthesized as the infection progresses. Hepatitis A usually does not lead to chronic hepatitis.

stem: You are managing a patient with acute hepatitis from Hepatitis B that has recently started antiviral medications. Which of the following indications on a blood test at the 6 month mark would suggest to the patient the patient’s condition has progressed to chronic hepatitis?

options.html: High levels of HBsAg, absence of anti-HBs, and the absence of IgM anti-HBc
Absence of HBsAg, and high levels of anti-HBs
High levels of HBsAg, the presence of IgM anti-HBc, and the absence of anti-HBs
High levels of HBsAg, and the presence of anti-HBs and the absence of IgM anti-HBc

answer:
The correct answer is A.

During acute hepatitis, the levels of HBsAg are high, and IgM anti-HbC are high as they arebeing produced to fight the initial infection. In chronic hepatitis the HBsAg levels are still high however IgM anti-HBc is not being produced (since the patient is beyond acute stage of the infection), and there is a lack of anti-HBs (more developed antibodies) to fight the infection.

stem: Ricky is a 34-year-old with a history of ongoing intravenous drug use and tobacco use. He presents to the emergency department with vomiting and fatigue. On history, he denies taking other medications or consuming alcohol, and testifies that he has never shared any needles with another user. Physical examination reveals jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly. Bloodwork ordered includes a standard liver panel that showed elevation of AST, ALT, ANA, and SMA. Based on the presentation and patient history, what is the most likely diagnosis? A. Hepatitis C infection B. Hepatitis D infection C. Autoimmune hepatitis D. Alcoholic hepatitis E. Cholecystitis
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The elevated AST and ALT suggest a liver pathology, ruling out cholecystitis and pancreatitis. The patient has a history of intravenous drug use, which may suggest a hepatitis C infection. However, the patient does not share injection needles, reducing the likelihood of hepatitis C. Hepatitis D is dependent upon a current or previous Hepatitis B infection. Alcoholic hepatitis is unlikely given that Ricky does not consume alcohol. The only remaining option is autoimmune hepatitis, which is further supported with increased ANA and SMA levels.

stem: A 50-year-old male presents to your clinic with fatigue, ascites and jaundiced skin. The patient explains how they have previously been diagnosed with ulcerative colitis a few years ago, but these symptoms have been recurrent for the past 8 months. Concerned for a liver pathology you order liver panel blood work which reveals elevated levels of bilirubin, ALP (Alkaline Phosphatase), and low AMA levels. The physician conducts an ERCP which reveals biliary strictures. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely? A. Wilson’s disease B. Primary biliary cholangitis C. Primary sclerosing cholangitis D. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
answer:
The correct answer is C.

This patient likely has primary sclerosing cholangitis as this is characterized by autoimmune directed inflammation at the large intra and extrahepatic ducts. Furthermore, this disease is more common in males than females and patients with this disorder are also likely to have Ulcerative Colitis. Wilson’s Disease is an accumulation of copper in the hepatocytes. Primary Biliary cholangitis is characterized by ductal damage of the smaller intrahepatic bile ducts and is more common in women. NAFLD is primarily a liver disorder and would be indicated by an elevation of the ALT/AST enzymes.

The correct answer is A, C, D.

Ursodiol is a treatment for primary biliary cholangitis. Antibiotics (and stents) are a treatment for primary sclerosing cholangitis. stem: In your rotation in internal medicine, your attending physician (a gastroenterologist) has instructed you to see four patients and assess if their chronic liver cirrhosis is compensated or decompensated. Which patient is considered compensated? A. Robert, who has had liver cirrhosis for 3 years and has recently developed nausea and vomiting. Physical examination reveals scleral icterus and a bilirubin of 63 µmol/L. B. Brennan, who was admitted to the GI ward after he presented to the emergency department with ruptured esophageal varices. Brennan has normocytic anemia. C. Derek, who presented with a distended abdomen. During an abdominal exam, percussion reveals shifting dullness when the patient changes positions. D. Dale, who presented with increased abdominal pain and massive splenomegaly (spleen extending past the midline of the abdomen).
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Decompensation occurs when the patient has one (or more) of the following: ascites, jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, or bleeding esophageal varices. Robert has jaundice (bilirubin levels above 51.3 µmol//L). Brennan has ruptured (bleeding) esophageal varices. Derek’s shifting dullness on percussion indicates ascites. Dale’s massive splenomegaly does not indicate decompensated cirrhosis.

answer:

These are the treatments for ascites. After life-style modifications, diuretics are common treatments for ascites, followed by serial paracentesis or TIPS. Wilson’s disease is a copper[1]storage disease, and not an iron-storage disease. For option B, NAFLD stands for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease - consuming this amount of alcohol could lead to alcoholic fatty liver disease. Lastly, cholestasis is indeed a cause of chronic liver disease, such as primary biliary cholangitis or primary sclerosing cholangitis.

stem: A patient presents to your clinic with jaundiced skin and overall feelings of malaise. The patient’s history gives no significant findings other than a recent diagnosis of Crohn's disease. An initial blood test displays the patient has normal levels of AST, ALT, ALP, GGT, but elevated levels of total bilirubin and reduced levels of direct Bilirubin. Which of the following pathologies is most likely for this patient? A. Dubin Johnson Syndrome B. Rotor Syndrome C. Vitamin B12 Deficiency D. Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The most likely diagnosis based on the initial investigations is Vitamin B12 Deficiency. The patient shows isolated levels of unconjugated bilirubin - thus DJS and Rotor syndrome which are causes of isolated elevated levels of conjugated bilirubin should not be considered. Among the remaining options a Vitamin B12 Deficiency is most likely as the patient was recently diagnosed with Crohn's disease which can lead to the malabsorption of Vitamin B12 in the ileum and consequently ineffective erythropoiesis.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Ultrasound is a good first test to assess for gallbladder-related pathologies, as gallstones show up readily. CT may be necessary depending on the results of an ultrasound. A liver biopsy is invasive and other imaging modalities should be performed first. Finally, cholecystectomy and Whipple’s procedure are very invasive surgeries - more diagnostic tests would be required before these extensive maneuvers.

The correct answer is C.

The ileum is the location of reabsorption of bile salts and other fatty vitamins. When a Crohn’s flare-up occurs at the ileum, reduced reabsorption of bile salts and absorption of fatsoluble vitamins would lead to steatorrhea.

Hepatocellular carcinoma B. Hepatoblastoma C. Focal nodular hyperplasia D. Hemangioma
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Hepatoblastoma is the primary liver cancer in children. It’s characterized by anorexia/weight loss and enlarged abdomen, along with elevated levels of serum AFP. The treatment for AFP typically involves downstaging with chemotherapy/radiation followed by surgical resection.

stem: Which of the following hepatic masses is typically not a cause for concern and does not require intervention? A. Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma B. Focal nodular hyperplasia C. Beta-catenin activated hepatic adenoma D. Hepatoblastoma
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Hepatoblastoma and Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma are malignant neoplasms require treatment. Hepatic adenoma is typically benign; however, they can be characterized by their molecular profile – Beta-Catenin activated hepatic adenoma has a high risk of malignant transformation and may require surgical resection to prevent future malignancies. Furthermore, larger hepatic adenomas are at increased risk of hemorrhage. Focal Nodular Hyperplasia are benign lesions that are often incidentally – treatment is not recommended.

They also mention how in the past they underwent an Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). You have a strong suspicion of gallstone induced acute pancreatitis – which of the following findings would be most suggestive of this (instead of another pathology)? Choose the best answer. A. Elevated Amylase levels B. Elevated Lipase levels C. Elevated ALP levels D. Elevated CRP levels
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Pancreatitis is investigated on a blood test by looking at levels of Amylase and Lipase levels, however elevated Lipase levels are more specific to pancreatitis, whereas elevated Amylase levels can have multiple differential diagnoses (salivary gland disorders, renal failure, etc.). Elevated ALP may suggest bile duct pathologies, but the possibility of gallstones (which is a risk associated with ERCP) should be investigated with an MRCP or Ultrasound.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography D. Alcohol cessation
answer:
The correct answer is C.

ECRP is not a warranted management technique in this scenario as the patient’s chronic pancreatitis does not arise from a duct obstruction (due to gallstones). The correct answer is B.

Acute pancreatitis has a clinical presentation of sharp epigastric pain, but so does gallstones and inflammation of the gallbladder. He has risk factors for both acute pancreatitis (excessive alcohol consumption) and gallstones (excess cholesterol intake from fast food), however his ALP levels are normal, indicating no cholestatic pathology. Thus, the most likely diagnosis is acute pancreatitis caused by alcohol consumption.

stem: Which of the following sites of obstruction within the Biliary Tree would like lead to pancreatitis? A. Cystic duct B. Common bile duct C. Common hepatic duct D. Ampulla of Vater
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The pancreatic duct joins with the common bile duct at the Ampulla of Vater, where the pancreas releases pancreatic enzymes into the duodenum. If there is an obstruction at the Ampulla of Vater, pancreatic enzyme release will be obstructed, and this can lead to pancreatitis.

The correct answer is D.

Biliary atresia is a progressive fibroinflammatory process that can be fetal (onset shortly after birth) or acquired (onset 1-2 months after birth), and it is a gallbladder disease in infants. This is a rare condition that requires early diagnosis to prevent liver disease and death

stem: What are the ways that bowel obstruction can be differentiated from ascites?

options.html: Ascites presents with pain whereas bowel obstructions are painless
Ascites typically involves the upper abdomen whereas bowel obstruction involves the lower abdomen
Ascites on percussion has shifting dullness whereas bowel obstruction is tympanic throughout
Ascites present with bowel changes whereas bowel obstructions do not

answer:
The correct answer is C.

You may remember from clinical skills that ascites can be tested by percussion. Laying supine, the side of the patient’s abdomen is percussed medially until tympany is observed. Then, the patient is instructed to shift to a lateral decubitus position and percussion is repeated. If the location at which dullness changes to tympany changes (called shifting percussion), the patient has ascites.

stem: Jeffrey presented to the emergency room concerned about increasing lower-left- quadrant abdominal pain. On upright chest x-ray, the following was observed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Perforated diverticulitis and an ovarian tumour are on the list of differential diagnoses for lower left quadrant abdominal pain, along with colon cancer. Assuming our male patient Jeffrey does not have ovaries, this leaves perforated diverticulitis as the only possible option. The presence of free air in an upright chest X-ray further supports perforation of the bowels and is a medical emergency.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Obscure bleeding is characterized by bleeding that cannot be visualized by standard upper or lower endoscopy procedures. Small intestine bleeds generally cannot be visualized using these techniques and other techniques such as capsule endoscopy or the double balloon must be used.

His past medical history includes a past appendectomy and previous anterolateral myocardial infection and subsequent left ventricular aneurysm. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient given his presentation and past medical history?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Based on this presentation of pain out of proportion to physical exam findings, centrally located, this is indicative of a small bowel ischemia. Small bowel ischemia could be an arterial occlusive ischemia (rapid onset, caused by thrombolism or embolism), or a venous occlusive ischemia (gradual onset). His presence in the emergency room indicates a rapid onset. The patient’s history of left ventricular aneurysm also fits with this diagnosis, as this creates an environment within the heart for embolisms to develop.

Small bowel ischemia presents with pain out of proportion, has a high mortality and usually requires surgical management. answer:
The correct answer is C.

The 35-year-old patient presents with an acute (one week history of presenting illness) anal fissure – appropriate therapy would include stool softeners, NSAIDS, Sitz Bath. Chronic Anal Fissures are treated with medication such as Botox (to promote a relaxation of the anal canal), and sphincterotomy (surgery) if needed. Band ligation is effective therapy for internal hemorrhoids to cut off blood supply.

stem: A patient with a Grade II hemorrhoid that presents with pain on defecation and streaks of bright red blood when wiping is requesting what his options are to treat his pain. Which statement below is true?

options.html: Grade II means that the hemorrhoid prolapses and must be reduced manually
The hemorrhoid would not be palpable on a digital rectal examination
Initial treatment should include stool softeners and increased water consumption
All of the above are true

answer:
The correct answer is C.

A hemorrhoid with pain indicates an external hemorrhoid, which would absolutely be palpable on a digital rectal examination. A grade II hemorrhoid prolapses and is reduced spontaneously (without manual reduction). Until the hemorrhoid is grade IV (irreducible), surgery is not warranted, and the patient should try to soften his or her stool (via avoiding dehydration and taking stool softeners like fiber or PEG3350) to make defecation easier.

stem: Todd the toddler was recently diagnosed with Milk Protein Intolerance (MPI). Which of the following statements is true?

options.html: Children with MPI often present with failure to thrive and appear lethargic/inactive
MPI is predominantly a secretory cause of diarrhea
MPI therapy necessitates that mothers switch from breastfeeding to formula
Children with MPI can present with bloody streaks and mucus in their stool

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Children with MPI often appear to be healthy and meet normal growth parameters. MPI is primarily an osmotic cause of diarrhea, as the undigested carbohydrates draws water into the lumen. MPI therapy does not necessitate that mothers switch to formula – children with MPI are unable to digest the COW milk protein. Children with MPI who are breastfed must remove other sources of dairy and soy from their diet.

stem: A physician attends to a 3-year-old boy with a 6-month history of constipation. After taking a history with the family and a thorough physical exam, the physician has a strong suspicion of mild functional constipation. Which of the following is an appropriate next management step?

options.html: Order an abdominal X-ray to confirm diagnosis of functional constipation
Order blood work to rule other causes and confirm diagnosis of functional constipation
Recommend the child incorporates more fluid and fiber and conduct a follow-up at an appropriate time
Discuss Toilet Hygiene to ensure the child only visits the bathroom when they need to go
Consider if a cleanout may be needed and prescribe an osmotic laxative

answer:
The correct answer is E.

A physical exam and a through history are enough for a diagnosis of functional constipation (no other investigations are necessary). Evidence shows that increasing fluid intake and fiber intake is not enough to resolve constipation. Toilet hygiene involves finding times (2-3 times a day) where the child can sit on toilet to anticipate a bowel movement in a non-punishment- oriented manner. A cleanout may be necessary, and it is common practice to prescribe an osmotic laxative such as PEG 335

stem: Which of the following type of contractions is a primary feature of sphincters?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Tonic contractions are prolonged contractions that are found in sphincters. During rest, sphincters remain contracted (closed) - as food starts approaching the sphincters, distension in the area signals ENS and CNS to inhibit contraction of smooth muscle cells, allowing food to pass through. Tonic contraction is also dependent on myogenic response of smooth muscle cells.

stem: A patients presents to the emergency room with hematochezia, and they are hemodynamically unstable. After checking their ABC’s, what is your next step in management?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Hematochezia is usually consistent with lower GI bleeding. However, in a hemodynamically unstable patient, upper GI bleeding could also present with hematochezia. Therefore, the first step should be performing an upper endoscopy (possibly accompanied by an angiography) to rule out massive bleeding in the upper GI tract. You cannot perform a colonoscopy on an unstable patient as bowel prep requires a day in advance.

Therefore, she should start colonoscopy 10 years younger than the age of diagnosis of her mother and it should be repeated every 5 years if negative. stem: Jada Pinkett Smith presents to the ER with involuntary guarding, rebound tenderness, and pain to percussion. A preliminary diagnosis of peritonitis is made. To confirm this diagnosis, which of the following investigations should be ordered? (Select all that apply)

options.html: Liver enzymes and liver function tests

answer:
The correct answer is A, B, D, E, G.

A CBC should be ordered to investigate the possibility of anemia and/or an infectious etiology. A pelvic ultrasound and HCG test are needed to rule out ectopic pregnancy. An abdominal X-Ray series can offer clues to a potential diagnosis, as would liver enzymes and liver function tests. A chest CT, urease breath test, and colonoscopy do not fit as well with the clinical picture described here. They are not included in the investigation of peritonitis.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Ascites is typically painless or presents with mild abdominal pain. Contrarily, bowel obstructions are painful. They present with central distention, tympany throughout upon percussion, central distention, nausea/vomiting, constipation, and obstipation.

A patient that is unfit for surgery should be hospitalized and put on IV antibiotics. stem: The upper half of the stomach is functionally designed for
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The function of the stomach can be thought of in terms of halves. The lower half of the stomach is primarily responsible for pumping and grinding, metering, peristalsis, and solid emptying. The upper half is primarily responsible for storage of food (acting as a reservoir), stomach contractions, and fluid emptying. Both the upper and lower halves are responsible for acid secretion, as this occurs in the body of the stomach.

stem: Acid secretion in the stomach comes from what cell type?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Parietal cells are the specialized acid-secreting cells of the stomach. These cells respond to histamine, gastrin, and acetylcholine receptor activation to produce acid. In addition to acid secretion, parietal cells also secrete intrinsic factor. Note that in the antrum, G cells (B) secrete gastrin (hormone, not a local factor). Goblet cells (C) secrete mucin. Chief cells (D) secrete pepsinogen and other enzymes.

stem: H+/K+ ATPase transporters found in parietal cells are the target sites of which heartburn medication?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Antacids are used to neutralize the acidity of stomach acid or to block acid secretion by gastric cells. Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, inhibiting the H+/K+ ATPase transporters. Bismuth (ie. Pepto-Bismol) works as a weak antacid and coats the stomach to protect the lining. Finally, H2 antagonists work by blocking the action of histamine on parietal cells, decreasing acid production.

stem: What is the leading cause of gastric ulcers?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

NSAIDs are the leading cause of gastric ulcers. The pathogenesis of NSAID-induced gastric ulcers is related to the disruption of protective factors such as mucin production and prostaglandin secretion. NSAIDs directly inhibit prostaglandin production, and may exert indirect effects on mucin production. In vulnerable populations such as the elderly and hospitalized patients, whose existing protective factors may already be compromised, NSAID overuse is a significant iatrogenic problem as it can lead to unnecessary ulcer formation.

stem: Which of the following are complications of peptic ulcer disease?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Peptic ulcer disease can present with obstruction, perforation and hemorrhage. It can also mimic other gastrointestinal diseases. Obstruction usually occurs at the gastric outlet due to ulcers of the antropylorus or duodenum. Perforation and hemorrhage may occur wherever ulceration becomes severe. A helpful mnemonic to remember the complications of PUD is HOPP (last P is penetration).

stem: Quadruple therapy to eradicate H. pylori refers, in general, to which combination of drugs?

options.html: One PPI, one H2 antagonist, amoxicillin and tetracycline

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Quadruple therapy for H. Pylori eradication includes a proton pump inhibitor and either 1) bismuth, Metronidazole and tetracycline (PBMT) OR 2) amoxicillin, metronidazole, and clarithromycin (PAMC) . The proton pump inhibitor most often used is omeprazole although pantoprazole or rabeprazole are also used. If eradication fails, PAL (PPI, amoxicillin, levofloxacin) or PAR (PPI, amoxicillin, rifabutin) are options.

The epiploic foramen (omental foramen) is the connection between the greater sac and the lesser sac of the abdomen. It is bordered by the hepatoduodenal ligament, the peritoneum of the IVC, the peritoneum of the caudate lobe of the liver and the peritoneum of the duodenum.

stem: What of the following is the least common origin of GI bleeds?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Rationally evaluating this list can save you from unnecessary memorization. We can eliminate stomach (A) and the first stage duodenum (D) as these are the common sites of peptic ulcers, which are a common problem (not to mention gastric varices and many other causes). Likewise, we can eliminate the colon (B) because it is the most common site of lower GI bleeds. We must now decide between the cecum and the jejunum. Small bowel bleeds outside of the first stage duodenum and the terminal ileum rare. In contrast, the cecum (E) is part of the colon and at the junction of the terminal ileum, two sites where bleeding is more common than the jejunum. Alternatively, you could memorize the relative frequency of GI bleeds by location, and you would see that mid- small bowel is the least frequent, and thus jejunum (C) is the correct answer.

stem: What is a possible complication of a choledochal cyst?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

A choledochal cyst is a congenital dilation of the common bile duct. The dilation predisposes the duct to bile stasis allowing for infection to occur. Infection can cause stricture formation, stone formation (bacteria deconjugate the bile acids), as well as cause metaplasia, dysplasia, and finally carcinoma.

stem: What is the pathogenesis of the development of carcinoma from a choledochal cyst?

options.html: Bile stasis → deconjugated bile acids → bacteria overgrowth → metaplasia → dysplasia →cancer

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Dilation of the bile duct predisposes to the duct to bile stasis. Bile stasis permits bacteria growth within the duct and as the bacteria proliferate they deconjugate the bile acids. Deconjugated bile within the duct system, along with infection and inflammation, lead to metaplastic changes within the cells forming the duct. Metaplastic changes lead to dysplastic changes, and finally full blown carcinoma (cholangiocarcinoma) can occur.

stem: Which structure would bleed if cut in surgery?
answer: C) Lateral umbilical fold. The median umbilical fold is the obliterated urachus (the urachus is a remnant of the allantois which sends waste to the placenta during the first 7 weeks gestation. Once the cloaca ruptures and starts dumping waste into the amniotic fluid, there is no need for the allantois for waste removal and it obliterates into the urachus). The medial umbilical fold is the obliterated umbilical artery (during development the umbilical artery carries deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta, after birth once the neonate is breathing on its own the vasculature connection to mom is obliterated). The lateral umbilical fold contains the inferior epigastric vessels (which would bleed if cut). The superior umbilical fold does not exist.

stem: Which of the following is FALSE about slow wave electrical activity in the GI tract?

options.html: It is dependent on innervation from the enteric nervous system
Slow wave refers to the spontaneous variation at rest of the muscle fibre

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Slow waves are not dependent on innervation by the enteric nervous system, so A is false. This is because the slow waves are spontaneous variations in the membrane potential of the smooth muscle fibres at rest (D). These spontaneous variations of muscle are therefore independent of nervous system activity. Answers B and C are also correct. The ICC coordinate their pacing of slow waves to ensure GI tract contents are propagated away from the mouth (B). Although the ICC cannot generate a contraction, they coordinate contractions by determining the frequency and timing of slow waves, which are in turn required for an action potential or a contraction to occur (C).

stem: Which of the following is not a possible pathophysiology of Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

An inflammatory response is not a characteristic of IBS. IBS is a functional disorder; this means that no true organic etiology can be found. Inflammation of the bowel would be more in keeping with an organic disease such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) rather than IBS. stem: In colorectal cancer:

Left sided cancers present with obvious bleeding or obstruction
FOB screening is recommended annually for all individuals 70 years and older
In most cases, there is a short interval between polyp development and cancer

Whereas right sided cancers typically present with non-GI symptoms such as weight loss and anemia, left-sided cancers generally present with more typical GI symptoms, largely due to the smaller lumen of the left-sided colon allowing for easier obstruction. stem: What is the most common indication for liver transplantation in children?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

While there are many conditions that can lead to liver transplantation in children, the leading cause is extrahepatic biliary atresia. It can be congential or acquired. In the congenital form, it is a birth defect where the bile duct is blocked or absent. With the acquired form, the patients usually have autoimmune disease. Generally, children will have progressive cholestasis with the associated features of jaundice, pruritus, malabsorption with growth retardation, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies, etc.

stem: A 5-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. On examination, the child appears pale and dehydrated. Laboratory tests reveal hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, consistent with a diagnosis of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). What is the appropriate management for this patient? Select all that apply.
answer: The correct options are A), C), and D). Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a potentially life-threatening condition characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. It is most commonly caused by Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) infection, which is often associated with diarrhea. A) Fluid resuscitation is a critical initial management step for HUS to maintain adequate organ perfusion and prevent further renal injury. B) Antibiotics are not routinely recommended for HUS caused by STEC infection. In fact, some studies suggest that antibiotics may actually increase the risk of HUS development by increasing the release of Shiga toxin. C) Blood transfusion may be necessary to correct severe anemia and maintain adequate oxygen delivery to the tissues. D) Dialysis may be necessary in patients with severe acute kidney injury and fluid overload. E) Antidiarrheals are not recommended in HUS because they may prolong the duration of bacterial shedding and increase the risk of complications. F) Platelet transfusion is not typically necessary in HUS because thrombocytopenia is usually mild and self-limited. In fact, platelet transfusion may increase the risk of thrombotic complications.

stem: Which of the following are not a common cause of acute pancreatitis:
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Alcohol (A) is a classic cause of acute pancreatitis (easy to remember with the I GET SMASHED mnemonic), as alcohol is directly toxic to acinar cells. The other classic and the most common cause is gallstones (C) which can cause acute pancreatitis by blocking the outflow of pancreatic secretions, leading to autodigestion of the pancreas. Hypertriglyeridemia (D) is one of the metabolic causes of acute pancreatitis, along with hypercalcemia and hyperlipidemia. Autoimmune diseases (E) such as polyarteritis nodosa and systemic lupus erythematosus can also cause acute pancreatitis. A pulmonary embolism alone does not cause acute pancreatitis.

stem: You are in the Emergency Room when a 45 year old man arrives presenting with vague RUQ pain. You notice he is slightly jaundiced during inspection and upon physical exam he demonstrates tenderness in the right upper quadrant. In your investigation, you order Hepatitis B serology. The results come back as: -ve HBsAg, +ve anti-HBs, +ve anti-HBe, +ve anti-HBc, -ve HBeAg. What does this say about his condition.

options.html: He has been vaccinated and immunized against HepB previously but never got it
He has had an acute flare of HepB.
He has not been immunized against HepB nor has gotten the disease in the past
He is a chronic carrier of HBV

answer:
The correct answer is A.

HbsAg is a marker of acute or chronic infection; since this is negative, this individual does not currently have a Hepatitis B infection. anti-HBc is the antibody against the core protein, which indicates that this individual had a previous exposure (because we know he/she is not infected now). From these two findings alone, we can answer the question (A - previously infected). anti-HBs is positive, but could be positive if someone had recovered from an infection or had been vaccinated. anti-HBe is positive, which means this person has clinically recovered from a Hep B infection and is immune (since we know she/he is not currently infected). HBeAg is negative, which means this person is not infective at present, consistent with our previous findings.

stem: In primary biliary cirrhosis, which antibody investigation is found to be positive in over 95% of the individuals with PBC.
answer:
The correct answer is D.

In 95% of individuals, anti-mitochondrial antibodies are found. Although the other antibodies listed may be positive in other autoimmune diseases, anti-mitochondrial antibodies have high sensitivity and specificity for PBC.

stem: In cases of hepatocellular carcinoma, extrahepatic sites of metastases are most commonly found in.
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Hepatocellular carcinoma most frequently spreads hematogenously to other sites of the body, most notably the lungs. The predilection for the lungs is unsurprising given that the liver is highly vascular, and blood from the hepatic veins travels to the IVC → RA → RV → lungs before anywhere else.

stem: The most common form of malignant tumor in the liver is:
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The question asks for the most common malignant neoplasm in the liver, which is metastatic cancer from elsewhere in the body. The most common benign neoplasms (from high to low): hemangioma (A) and hepatic adenoma. The most common malignant neoplasms arising from the liver: hepatocellular carcinoma, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, and angiosarcoma (in order from highest to lowest incidence). In kids, the most common malignant neoplasm arising from the liver is hepatoblastoma.

stem: A 26-year-old man walks into Emergency Room complaining of right upper quadrant pain, itching, and a fever. On examination you find a large palpable liver, as well as a firm spleen tip. He doesn’t appear jaundiced. Blood tests show AST of 42 and ALT of 48 but elevated levels of alkaline phosphatase of 665. His family has a history of inflammatory bowel disease and he has a previous diagnosed history of ulcerative colitis. What is the most likely diagnosis.
answer:
The correct answer is E.

When you encounter a case of a young male with inflammatory bowel disease presenting with symptoms such as pruritis, RUQ, and/or fever, you should immediately think primary sclerosing cholangitis. PSC has an 80% association with IBD (especially ulcerative colitis). It is an autoimmune disease in which the bile ducts become destroyed (cholestatic liver disease).

stem: A 47 year old woman comes into your clinic with complaints of severe dull epigastric pain which comes after each meal. She is afebrile and not jaundiced. She has a 18 year history of alcoholism and a recent alcoholic binge. On physical exam you note slight diffuse tenderness across the abdomen, she was negative for Murphy's sign. Her blood work showed normal bilirubin and mildly elevated ALT, AST, ALP. What is the appropriate first line imaging modality?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

An abdominal U/S is the best imaging modality in this case due to several reasons. An abdominal U/S will give you a general idea of how this patient’s abdomen will look, including all the organs in the area. It is cheap, fast, and removes the need for the patient to be exposed unnecessarily to radiation. You are also able to look at the soft tissue structures of the region, including details of the biliary tree, check for signs of inflammation, obstruction, or stones. You are not able to do this in such detail with abdominal X-ray, HIDA, or ERCP. Without further indications, abdominal CT would also be inappropriate.

stem: A 16-year-old adolescent female shows up to the ER with fatigue and mild jaundice. She denies fever and is afebrile. On examination she has a mildly enlarged liver. Her blood work shows mildly elevated liver enzymes, bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase. She has a positive antinuclear antibody. Which of following conditions is most likely for her presentation.
answer:
The correct answer is E.

The key features to this patient’s presentation are: she is female, mildly jaundiced, elevated AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, and a positive ANA. Given these features, this patient is most likely suffering from autoimmune hepatitis. Several of the other options can be ruled out, such as primary sclerosing cholangitis (D) (mostly young men, not women). Hemochromatosis (B) is more likely to present with bronzing of the skin, and older than 16 in women because of menstruation (natural phlebotomy, if you will). In Wilson’s disease (A), you would not expect autoimmune markers to be positive, and there would be a salient family history of psychiatric illness.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

stem: A 24 year old medical clinical clerk is accidentally stuck with a hollow needle while she is performing a procedure on the ward on a Hepatitis B positive patient. She goes to get blood work which comes back: HBsAg negative, HBsAb positive, HBcAb negative, HBeAg negative, and HBeAb negative. Which of the following regarding the student’s hepatitis status is true?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The Hepatitis B vaccine confers antibody immunity against the surface antigen; this patient only has HBsAb positivity, consistent with the antibody against the surface antigen but no prior exposure. Had this patient been exposed or acutely infected, at least one antigen would be positive (HBsAg or HBeAg).

stem: A 54-year-old man comes in presenting with jaundice and dark urine. He has a 12 pack of beer per day alcohol drinking history. Lab results come in with AST 400, ALT 250, alkaline phosphatase 120, total bilirubin of 31 µg/L, and direct bilirubin of 12 µg/L. What is his most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Alcoholic hepatitis is most likely given the heavy drinking history presented. Additionally, his AST is greater than his ALT and both are under 500, which is a common set of lab results for alcoholic hepatitis. Gilbert’s syndrome (B) would be characterized by stress-induced jaundice, normal liver enzymes, and a high total but low direct bilirubin, probably 20% or less of the total. While hemolysis (C) may present with elevated bilirubin, it’s less likely given the elevated liver enzymes and history. Viral hepatitis (E) would present with an ALT>AST, and generally both would be elevated past 1000.

stem: A 43-year-old woman with a BMI of 36 presents with severe, severe dull epigastric pain after eating. She is afebrile, has mild scleral icterus, and moderate diffuse tenderness on palpation of abdomen. Her blood work comes back with AST 210, ALT 180, Alkaline Phosphatase 400, total bilirubin 35, direct bilirubin 18. What is her most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Of all of the options, cholecystitis is the most consistent with this patient’s presentation of epigastric pain after eating. Remember that PSC (C) is more common in men, pancreatic cancer (A) is usually not painful until the very late stages of disease if at all, and that we would expect other symptoms and no association with eating if this patient had either Churg-Strauss (D) or Budd-Chiari (E).

stem: A 57-year-old man with a longstanding history of alcohol use, as well as a past medical history of HCV is found by his daughter in a drowsy state from which he decreased awareness of his surroundings as well as delayed response to questions and stimulation. He also has mild asterixis. Currently he is on coversyl, lactulose, and neomycin. What is the diagnosis

options.html: Delirium secondary to hepatocellular carcinoma brain metastasis

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Of the options presented, hepatic encephalopathy secondary to alcohol intoxication is the most likely cause of his symptoms. The decreased LOC and asterixis are caused by the accumulation of ammonia and other toxins in the blood after liver failure. The history of hepatitis C would have predisposed him to both encephalopathy and hepatocellular carcinoma (B) but HCC doesn’t commonly spread to the brain. None of his meds have hepatic or neurological side effects (A), kernicterus generally only occurs in jaundiced newborns (D) and delirium (E) tremens is acute, severe alcohol withdrawal characterized by fevers, seizures, autonomic dysfunction, sweating, and eventually coma and death.

stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in North American adults?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Alcoholism is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in North American adults, causing >90% of cases. This is due to the changes in the pancreas caused by alcohol, including the increased viscosity of the pancreatic juices, decreased pancreatic secretion of pancreatic stone protein, and acinar and duct cell toxicity. Unusual causes include CF, severe protein-calorie malnutrition, hereditary and idiopathic reasons. Gallstones only cause acute pancreatitis, not chronic cases.

stem: What is not a possible complication of choledocholithiasis?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Complications of choledocholithiasis include bile duct stricture, cholangitis, pancreatitis, and biliary cirrhosis. However, it does not cause acute cholecystitis because by definition, cholecystitis is an inflammation of the gallbladder resulting from sustained gallstone impaction in the cystic duct or Hartmann’s pouch, whereas choledocholithiasis involves stones in the common bile duct, further down the tract.

options.html: Metastases of the colorectal cancer to the gallbladder

stem: A 35-year-old female patients presents in the emergency with a 3 day history of severe epigastric pain that radiates to her back along with nausea, vomiting, and fever. You immediately suspect acute pancreatitis and order lab-work to confirm your diagnosis. The results come back as (normal ranges in brackets): Hb 133 (120-160), WBC 18 (4-11), lipase 16000 (<150), ALT 19 (<20), AST 37 (<35), ALP 116 (50-160), random glucose 12 (4.0-7.8), LDH 203 (50-150). Which of the above values is the LEAST predictive of you patient’s mortality with acute pancreatitis?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Based on Ranson’s Criteria for acute pancreatitis, it is useful to look at the following five factors at time of admission to predict the course of the disease. They are a) Age >55yrs, b) WBC >16, c) Glucose >11, d)LDH >350, and e) AST >250. Thus, while lipase is a useful investigative tool, it is not necessarily helpful as a predictive value.

stem: Which of the following does not have the potential to cause conjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Gilbert’s disease is a problem of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not conjugated. This is because the enzyme responsible for conjugation is sluggish or deficient. Pregnancy (A) can lead to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, usually early in pregnancy as a benign recurrence of cholestasis, or late in pregnancy as acute fatty liver of pregnancy or preeclampsia. Miliary TB (C) can cause obstruction of bile outflow (among other multi-organ problems) that would present with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Pancreatic cancer (D) can lead to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia if, for instance, the tumour compresses the bile duct. Biliary atresia (E) is a common cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in infancy.

stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor for cholelithiasis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Females are more prone to cholelithiasis than males as estrogen is an important risk factor. In addition, obesity and being <50y/o (Age) also are risk factors. Being on TPN causes impaired gallbladder emptying, thus facilitating stone formation, and rapid weight loss cause rapid cholesterol mobilization and biliary stasis which can also increase the chances of gallstone development. A common way to think about the risk factors for gallstones is the 4F’s: Fat, Female, Fertile, Forties.

stem: A 65-year old male with a long history of alcoholism presents to Emergency with delirium. After speaking to his wife, you learn that he became more and more confused over past week after going on an alcohol binge. A quick exam reveals a lethargic, but arousable, man who is disoriented with an abdomen bulging bilaterally at the flanks. The liver is palpable. What would be the most appropriate treatment for his condition?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

The history of alcohol abuse and his symptoms suggest hepatic encephalopathy. Lactulose is metabolized by gut bacteria into lactic and acetic acid, acidifying the gut. Ammonia excreted (NH3) is then trapped in its ionized form ammonium (NH4+), preventing resorption and decreasing the concentration of ammonia in the blood.

stem: A 47-year-old Caucasian woman comes to your clinic with a complaint of weight loss, epigastric pain, and diarrhea with foul smelling stool that started “a little while ago”. She also notes that she’s concerned about the weight loss but just seems to be turned off food as eating seems to make the pain worse. Bloodwork reveal hyperglycemia and elevated INR. She denies smoking but admits to regular alcohol consumption. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The most likely cause of this patient’s presentation is chronic pancreatitis. Clues to this diagnosis include: chronic alcohol use; persistent epigastric pain; diarrhea, foul-smelling stools, and weight loss, all of which can be attributed to poor fat digestion due to insufficient pancreatic enzyme secretion or production; and apparent diabetes, which can result from severe cases of chronic pancreatitis in which the beta cells are destroyed or cannot produce enough insulin. T2DM (A) or Celiac disease (B) on their own are not enough to explain the constellation of symptoms, although malabsorption and hyperglycemia are features of this patient’s presentation. Peptic ulcer disease (D) would explain her epigastric pain relating to meals, but would present with anemia and black stools, rather than diabetes and foul-smelling stools. A bowel obstruction (E) is also inconsistent with the symptoms, and would likely feature bilious vomiting.

stem: Which of the following statements accurately describes the anatomical relationship between the portal vein and the hepatic artery?

options.html: The portal vein is located anterior to the hepatic artery.
The portal vein and the hepatic artery run parallel to each other throughout their course.
The portal vein and the hepatic artery run adjacent to each other in a common sheath.
The portal vein and the hepatic artery have no anatomical relationship and do not share a common pathway.

answer: C) The portal vein and the hepatic artery run adjacent to each other in a common sheath. Explanation: The portal vein and the hepatic artery are the two main vessels that supply blood to the liver. While they do not directly communicate with each other, they are intimately related in their course to the liver. The portal vein is formed by the union of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins and runs adjacent to the hepatic artery in a common sheath as they enter the liver. This close anatomical relationship is important in the regulation of blood flow to the liver and helps to ensure that the liver receives adequate oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery and nutrient-rich blood from the portal vein.

stem: Which of the following laboratory findings is most commonly associated with cirrhosis
answer: D) Elevated levels of bilirubin Explanation: Cirrhosis is a chronic liver disease characterized by progressive scarring and fibrosis of the liver tissue. As liver function declines in cirrhosis, there is impaired processing and excretion of bilirubin, leading to elevated levels of this pigment in the blood. Bilirubin is a waste product produced by the breakdown of red blood cells, and high levels can cause yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice). While elevated levels of AST and ALT can also be seen in liver disease, they are not specific to cirrhosis and can be elevated in many types of liver injury. Elevated levels of ALP can be seen in liver disease as well as bone disease and other conditions, and are not specific to cirrhosis.

stem: In hepatitis B infection, which of the following hepatitis B virus (HBV) serological markers indicates a chronic infection?

options.html: HBsAg positive, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs negative
HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs positive
HBsAg positive, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs positive
HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negative, anti-HBs negative

answer: A) HBsAg positive, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs negative Explanation: In hepatitis B infection, the presence of HBV serological markers can indicate the different stages of infection. HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen) is the first serological marker to appear and indicates acute infection. If HBsAg persists for more than 6 months, it indicates chronic infection. Anti-HBc (hepatitis B core antibody) is a marker of previous or ongoing infection with HBV, and can be positive in both acute and chronic infection. Anti-HBs (hepatitis B surface antibody) is a marker of immunity to HBV and is produced in response to vaccination or past infection. In chronic hepatitis B infection, the patient is HBsAg positive for more than 6 months, anti-HBc positive, and anti-HBs negative. In the other options, the patient is either not infected (D), has recovered from past infection or been vaccinated (B), or has an unclear stage of infection (C).

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with fatigue, joint pain, and abnormal liver function tests. Further evaluation reveals elevated serum ferritin levels and genetic testing confirms a diagnosis of hemochromatosis. What is the recommended treatment for this patient?
answer: B) Phlebotomy Explanation: Hemochromatosis is a hereditary disorder characterized by excessive accumulation of iron in the body, leading to tissue damage and organ dysfunction. The primary treatment for hemochromatosis is phlebotomy (bloodletting), which aims to remove excess iron from the body. In the initial phase of treatment, weekly or biweekly phlebotomy is recommended until iron levels are reduced to normal levels. Once normal iron levels are achieved, the frequency of phlebotomy can be decreased to every few months to maintain normal iron levels. Iron supplementation (A) is contraindicated in hemochromatosis as it can exacerbate iron overload. Corticosteroids (C) may be used in certain cases of hemochromatosis-related liver disease, but they are not the primary treatment. Chelation therapy (D), which is commonly used to treat iron overload in thalassemia, is not effective in hemochromatosis as it does not remove iron from the liver.

stem: Which of the following are contraindications to transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)? There may be more than one correct answer.
answer: A) Hepatic encephalopathy and D) Severe coagulopathy Explanation: TIPS is a procedure that involves creating a shunt between the portal vein and hepatic vein to reduce portal hypertension in patients with cirrhosis and related complications. However, TIPS is not suitable for all patients, and there are several contraindications to the procedure. Hepatic encephalopathy is a common complication of cirrhosis and is a contraindication to TIPS as it can worsen after the procedure. Severe coagulopathy, such as an INR greater than 2.5, is also a contraindication to TIPS as the procedure can lead to bleeding complications. Severe pulmonary hypertension (B) is not a direct contraindication to TIPS, but it can increase the risk of complications during the procedure. Advanced liver cirrhosis (C) is also not a direct contraindication, but it can decrease the efficacy of the procedure and increase the risk of complications.

stem: A 55-year-old male presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain that radiates to his back, vomiting, and fever. Laboratory testing reveals elevated serum lipase and amylase levels. CT scan demonstrates pancreatic inflammation and fluid collections. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
answer: B) Pancreatitis Explanation: The patient's symptoms and laboratory findings are highly suggestive of acute pancreatitis, which is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas that can be caused by various factors, including alcohol consumption, gallstones, high triglyceride levels, infections, and certain medications. Abdominal pain is the hallmark symptom of pancreatitis and is often severe and persistent, radiating to the back. Nausea, vomiting, fever, and elevated serum lipase and amylase levels are common features of pancreatitis. CT scan is a valuable imaging modality to confirm the diagnosis and assess the severity of the disease. Pancreatic cancer (A) typically presents with more subtle symptoms and is often detected at a later stage when the disease has already spread. Pancreatic pseudocyst (C) is a complication of chronic pancreatitis and presents with a palpable abdominal mass and obstructive symptoms. Pancreatic duct obstruction (D) can cause chronic pancreatitis, but it is not the primary cause of acute pancreatitis.

stem: Which of the following is not used to diagnose obstructive ascending cholangitis?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Reynold’s pentad consists of shock, altered mental status, jaundice, fever, and abdominal pain. Emesis (A) is not part of this list, whereas hypotension (shock) (B), altered mental status (C), jaundice (D), and fever (E) are. (Reynold’s Pentad is perhaps easiest to remember as Charcot’s triad + altered mental status and shock.)

stem: Which of the following is not a symptom of functional dyspepsia?

options.html: A four months history of recurrent upper abdominal pain

answer:
The correct answer is E.

Functional dyspepsia is a functional, or non-organic disorder. All of the other options (recurrent upper abdominal pain, no relief passing stool, nausea, bloating, and early satiety) do not specifically implicate a functional or organic cause. GI bleeding is NOT a functional problem but an organic one, and therefore cannot be part of the symptom complex for a functional disorder.

stem: A patient presents to the ER with obstipation and colicky abdominal pain. After a series of investigations the physician provides a diagnosis of small bowel obstructions. Which of the following is an appropriate intial treatment
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Small Bowel obstructions require conservative management which include a nasogastric tube for suction to decompress the stomach and relieve nausea and vomiting. If the SB does not resolve after 48 hours surgical management is often indicated. For a large bowel obstruction, surgery is the first line of treatment.

stem: A 65-year-old female presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain, distention, and vomiting. On examination, she has hyperactive bowel sounds in the upper abdomen and hypoactive bowel sounds in the lower abdomen. What type of bowel obstruction is more likely in this patient?
answer: A) Small bowel obstruction Explanation: The clinical presentation of small bowel obstruction and large bowel obstruction can overlap, but there are certain features that can help distinguish between the two. Small bowel obstruction typically presents with more severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and rapid onset of symptoms, while large bowel obstruction may present with more chronic or intermittent symptoms such as constipation, bloating, and lower abdominal pain. On examination, hyperactive bowel sounds in the upper abdomen and hypoactive bowel sounds in the lower abdomen are more suggestive of a small bowel obstruction as the obstruction typically occurs proximal to the ileocecal valve. In contrast, a large bowel obstruction usually presents with high-pitched bowel sounds in the lower abdomen due to distension and accumulation of gas and stool. Gastric outlet obstruction (C) can cause similar symptoms to small bowel obstruction but typically presents with more prominent vomiting and epigastric pain. Colonic volvulus (D) is a type of large bowel obstruction that presents with colicky abdominal pain, obstipation, and distension, and may be associated with a palpable mass on examination.

stem: A 50-year-old male presents to the emergency department with left lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and nausea. On examination, there is tenderness and guarding in the left lower quadrant with no rebound tenderness. CT scan of the abdomen shows sigmoid colon diverticulitis without evidence of perforation or abscess. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
answer: B) Antibiotics alone Explanation: The clinical presentation of diverticulitis includes left lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, and change in bowel habits. CT scan is the imaging modality of choice for the diagnosis of diverticulitis and to assess for complications such as perforation or abscess. In cases of uncomplicated diverticulitis without evidence of perforation or abscess, the mainstay of treatment is antibiotics alone. Patients with mild to moderate symptoms can be treated on an outpatient basis, while those with severe symptoms or comorbidities may require hospitalization. Observation and supportive care (A) alone are not sufficient for the treatment of diverticulitis. Surgical consultation (C) may be needed in cases of complicated diverticulitis, but it is not indicated in uncomplicated cases. Percutaneous drainage of abscess (D) is indicated in cases of complicated diverticulitis with abscess formation. Colonoscopy (E) is contraindicated during an acute episode of diverticulitis, as it may increase the risk of perforation.

stem: Which of the following investigations would you choose for a patient with severe right lower quadrant abdominal pain that began in the umbilical region and migrated to the right side, with rebound tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis? (Pick 4)
answer: The correct answers include: A) Complete blood count (CBC) to assess for leukocytosis, which is commonly seen in patients with appendicitis B) Serum electrolytes to evaluate for dehydration or electrolyte imbalances D) Abdominal ultrasound (US) as the first-line imaging modality to confirm the diagnosis of appendicitis G) C-reactive protein (CRP) level to assess for inflammation in the body, which is typically elevated in patients with appendicitis These investigations are used in the workup of a patient with suspected appendicitis, as they help to confirm the diagnosis and assess for any complications that may arise.
